Edit one Pro Flash image at its unchanged native canvas size.

Supply image_url (preferred), image_base64, or an owned source_image_id.
method=text requires description; method=reference requires reference_image
({url}, {base64}, or {source_image_id}). References must fit the source canvas.
No-background defaults to the source's transparency. Optional palette
correction matches source colors. Query get_pro_flash_capabilities for exact
shapes. Returns one queued image; poll get_image(job_id), then download.

Cost: by the SOURCE canvas's longest side — 5 generations up to 96px, 6 from
100 to 208, 9 from 212 to 256, for one image. The same ladder as Pro Flash
create and inpaint, and cheaper than edit_image's 10/15/25 tier at every
size. get_pro_flash_capabilities(operation="edit", width=, height=) prices
an exact size for free.

reference_image.description: Exactly ONE of its three sources (`url` also accepts an `upload:<id>` from get_upload_url or a data: URL). Required when method='reference'. It must fit the edit canvas, which is the source image's own size because Pro Flash never rescales — crop it instead.

usage_description.description: How this reference should guide appearance.

no_background.description: Background removal on the result. Left out it follows the source: on if the source has any non-opaque pixel, off if it is fully opaque. Off, the edit is drawn on a plain white background, so a transparent sprite sent with false comes back flattened onto white.

use_color_palette_correction.description: Hold the edit to the SOURCE image's own colours: the prompt asks for them and every visible output pixel is then mapped to the nearest colour already in the source, so the edit introduces no new colour. Use it for a locked palette or a repair that must not recolour; leave it off when the edit needs a colour the source does not have (a red cape on a grey knight). Needs a source with visible pixels. Neither this tool nor inpaint_image_pro_flash takes a palette LIST - create_image_pro and image_to_pixelart_pro_flash are the Pro Flash tools that do.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__edit_map
tools.description:
Paint terrain on a map: rivers and roads with `path`, areas with `rect`.

You choose regions, not tiles — the tileset picks the actual tile art for
every corner, and shoreline rows between terrains are inserted for you. Name
a terrain the map doesn't have yet and the tileset providing it is attached
automatically, along with any tileset connected to it. A tileset not
connected to this map attaches only when you name its terrain exactly; it
meets the map with hard edges (straight seams) until a tileset joins them.

On a sidescroller map each terrain is a platform top ("grass", "snow") over
its body, and empty cells are air: paint the solid ground. Naming a top the
map lacks attaches the sidescroller tileset that has it.

Cost: free. Painting spends no generations however much you repaint — the
tileset it draws with was paid for when it was generated.

Returns what changed, an ASCII view of the affected area, and — when the edit
used new art or went wrong — a rendered image of it. Pass show=true to see
the image any time; use view_map to look at somewhere you did not just paint.

oneOf.description: A stroke through waypoints — rivers, roads, coastlines.
An axis-aligned area — fields, plazas, blocks of ground.

dry_run.description: Preview the result and warnings without saving

show.description: Also return a rendered IMAGE of the edited area. On by default whenever the edit brings in a terrain you have not seen rendered, or leaves tiles no tileset can draw.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__edit_map_areas
tools.description:
Declare what blocks movement, as Map Workshop's Gameplay Layers do.

Terrain says what a map LOOKS like; a gameplay layer says what it PLAYS
like. Without one the game falls back to reading the terrain's own names,
so a map is solid or open by accident of vocabulary.

A layer is linked to terrains rather than to an area: the exporter derives
the cells from the terrain grid every time the map is exported, so painting
more water extends the water layer by itself.

    edit_map_areas(map_id, action="add", name="Non-walkable",
                   terrains=["water"], walkable=false)

Call with no action to see the layers a map already has and what the game
makes of each one.

action.description: list the map's gameplay layers, or add/remove one

name.description: Layer name, for add and remove. The game reads the NAME as well as the tags, so name it for what it does: 'Non-walkable', 'Walkable'.

terrains.description: For add: the terrains this layer covers, by the names get_map shows (e.g. ["water","lava"]). The layer follows them — repaint the terrain and the collision follows, with no second edit here.

walkable.description: For add: true if the player can walk on these terrains, false if they block. Refused when the resulting layer would read the other way to the game, rather than writing one that plays wrong.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__estimate_skeleton
tools.description:
Estimate the skeleton of a humanoid sprite: its 18 joints, in exactly the
shape animate_with_skeleton_v3 takes.

Two calls: estimate_skeleton(image=...) queues it and returns a job id (usually
done in ~10-20 s, longer when the queue is busy); estimate_skeleton(job_id=...)
returns the keypoints once it is done (wait_for_jobs waits for it).

Pass the result as animate_with_skeleton_v3's `first_frame_keypoints` (the pose
the sprite is in), and use it as the starting point for each frame of
`keypoints` (the motion: move the joints frame by frame). x/y are fractions 0-1
of the image you sent; labels come in the order animate_with_skeleton_v3
lists them.

Humanoids only: the 18 joints are a person's. A fully transparent image is
refused before anything is charged.

Cost: 0.1 generations, charged when the estimate is done.

image.description: The character sprite, on a transparent background: `character:<id>:<direction>` (a rotation), `job:<id>` or `job:<id>:<index>` (an image tool result), `gallery:<id>`, `object:<id>[:<direction>]`, `upload:<id>`, a pixelart_workbench result id, an https or data URL of a PNG, or base64. One frame, up to 256x256; any size within that works (no padding needed).

job_id.description: The job id an earlier estimate_skeleton(image=...) returned: reads its keypoints once it is done. Pass image or job_id, not both.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__expand_object_to_8_directions
tools.description:
Turn one of your 1-direction objects into an 8-direction one, keeping the
same object: its id, tags and animations. Costs 10-25 generations by the
padded canvas (objects up to 168x168; larger ones are refused), ~2-4 min.

The new directions wait for review. get_object shows them (status
review-expansion) and the object stays 1-direction until you decide:
select_object_frames(object_id) with no indices keeps them (the canvas grows
to the review's size, animations move to existing_direction);
dismiss_review(object_id) discards them and leaves the object as it was.

To make a NEW 8-direction object from an image instead, use
create_8_direction_object(reference_image_base64=...).

object_id.description: Your completed 1-direction object (from list_objects or get_object).

existing_direction.description: Which way the object's current image faces. That image becomes this direction, unchanged, and the other 7 are drawn to match it. Ask the user if the image does not make it clear.

description.description: What the object is, to guide the new angles. Defaults to the object's own description.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__export_asset
tools.description:
Get a download link for a character or object as ZIP, spritesheet, .aseprite or GIF. Free.

The link needs no auth (the id is the key) and is fetched with plain HTTP,
e.g. `curl -fLo hero.aseprite <url>`. It answers 423 with Retry-After while
the asset or one of its animations is still generating.

asset_id.description: Id of the character or object.

format.description: zip: rotations + animation frames as PNGs (a character's ZIP holds every state; a 1-direction object without animations comes as its one PNG). spritesheet: one packed sheet + layout JSON. aseprite: one .aseprite file for this state. gif: the rotations turning, or one animation direction with animation_group_id.

animation_group_id.description: gif only: export this animation ([group: ...] id from get_character/get_object).

direction.description: gif only: the animation's direction (e.g. 'south'); optional when it has one.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__get_balance
tools.description: Check your account balance: remaining credits (USD) and subscription generations.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__get_character
tools.description:
Get character details, rotation URLs, animations, and download link.
Branches by status: processing (progress+ETA), failed (error+retry), completed (full data).

Download: three ways out, and the last one needs no HTTP at all.
`/mcp/characters/{id}/download` is a ZIP of every completed state in the
group — `?states=` narrows it, taking the state IDS this tool prints on
its `state:` lines, not their names — laid out as
`<state>/rotations/<direction>.png` and
`<state>/animations/<name>/<direction>/frame_000.png` (frame_NNN, 3 digits,
from 000), plus `<state>/portrait.png` and `<state>/vocal/grid.png` where
those exist, and a top-level `metadata.json` giving each state's size,
directions, view, template_id and a `frames` map listing every file — so
the per-direction frame counts are in there as the list lengths. A frame
storage lost shows up as `MISSING_FRAMES.txt` rather than a short ZIP.
`/mcp/characters/{id}/spritesheet` is a ZIP of one sheet PNG + its layout
JSON for THIS state only: row 0 is the rotations, then one row per
animation-direction, uniform cells sized to the largest frame with the rest
transparent padding (nothing is ever resized), and the JSON gives
`cell_size`, `sheet_size`, `columns`, `pivot: "cell-center"` and a row list
naming each row's animation, `animation_group_id`, direction and
frame_count.
To get the pixels back INLINE, with no download and nothing charged:
`pixelart_workbench(argv=["inspect", "character:<id>:<direction>:<animation>"])`
returns that animation's frames as one sheet image in the tool result, with
the canvas and frame durations — `<animation>` is the display name, type or
[group: ...] id this tool prints. `join ref ref --as rows` lays several
animations out one per row (sheets hold at most 1024 px a side).

character_id.description: Character UUID to retrieve

include_preview.description: Include preview image of south direction

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__get_font
tools.description:
Get a font result by job id.

Returns the glyph atlas (inline) + download URLs for the atlas PNG and the
.ttf if completed, or progress/error otherwise.

job_id.description: The job id returned by create_font.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__get_image
tools.description:
Get a raw-image result by job id, or a gallery image by `gallery:<id>`.

Returns the image(s) inline plus no-auth download URLs when completed, or
progress/error otherwise. A completed job also reports its gallery save:
the Creator ``asset_id`` once saved, or a failure note (the image is still
delivered) while the save is being retried.

job_id.description: The job id returned by any raw-image tool (create_image_pixflux, create_image_pixen, create_image_pro, edit_image, edit_image_pixen, transfer_outfit, inpaint_image, animate_image, image_to_pixelart, unzoom_image, correct_pixelart, reduce_colors, create_normal_map), or a gallery:<id> from list_images — images made on the website have no job id.

index.description: Return only this frame, inline. Use it to reach frames past the first few of a long animation without fetching a URL.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__get_isometric_tile
tools.description: Get an isometric tile by ID. Returns tile image and metadata if completed, or progress if processing.

tile_id.description: The UUID of the isometric tile to retrieve

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__get_lip_sync
tools.description:
Get the lip-sync frame plan for a line of dialogue — for animating in a game.

FREE, and nothing is rendered. Use this instead of create_talking_gif when the
game should animate the mouth itself: you get the spritesheet URL, the row for
the expression, and a frame list giving the column to draw and how long to hold
it. create_talking_gif is the better answer when you just want a playable file.

Timings are exact here — unlike a GIF, an engine can hold a frame for any
duration.

Example:
- get_lip_sync("<uuid>", "Welcome to the village, traveller!")

Returns immediately (no job to poll).

character_id.description: Character with a vocal animation (see create_vocal_animation). This tool is character-only on purpose: it hands the engine a spritesheet URL to load, and a portrait-only set has no stored spritesheet — for that case use create_talking_gif(from_job_id=...) instead.

text_to_speak.description: The line of dialogue to lip-sync.

mood.description: Which generated expression to use. Defaults to the character's first available expression.

frame_ms.description: Milliseconds to hold each mouth position.

hold_ms.description: Extra time on the final closed mouth.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__get_map
tools.description:
Show a map as an ASCII grid, one character per terrain cell.

With no crop you get the whole map downsampled to fit; pass x/y/width/height
for a 1:1 view of one area. Coordinates are terrain cells and can be
negative — the rulers show the real numbers, so read them off the view and
pass them straight to edit_map.

Maps built from tile groups (isometric, hex, oblique and similar tiles) show
their tile layers: for every cell the tile on top and the stack level it
sits on, plus each stacked column spelled out. Change those with
place_map_tiles.

export="godot" / "unity" / "pixellab" returns a download link for the map
as a game-engine project or the PixelLab ZIP instead of the view.

x.description: Crop: left edge, in terrain cells (q on tile layers)

y.description: Crop: top edge, in terrain cells (r on tile layers)

width.description: Crop width in cells

height.description: Crop height in cells

export.description: Instead of the view, get a download link for the map as Map Workshop's Export makes it: godot (Godot 4 project ZIP), unity (Unity 6 .unitypackage) or pixellab (PixelLab ZIP: map.json plus images, for custom engines). Free; the link needs no auth.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__get_map_object
tools.description:
Get map object status and data. Returns image if completed.
The object is permanent — place it on a map with place_map_object.
Retries saving finished pixels when B2 or database persistence failed.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__get_music
tools.description:
Check a song's status and get its audio link (MP3) once it is made.

Shows its style, lyrics and length; for a loop take, its loop points (play to
loop end, jump back to loop start).

song_id.description: A song_id from create_music or list_music

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__get_object
tools.description:
Get object details. Branches by status:
- processing: progress + ETA
- review: candidate frame URLs + inline previews
- expanding / review-expansion: an 8-direction expansion
  (expand_object_to_8_directions) running, then waiting to be kept or discarded
- completed: rotation URLs, animations, download link
- failed: error + retry hint

Download: `/mcp/objects/{id}/download` is a ZIP holding
`rotations/<direction>.png` and
`animations/<name>/<direction>/frame_000.png` (frame_NNN, 3 digits, from
000) at the ZIP root — flatter than the character ZIP, and with no
metadata.json. A one-direction object with no animations comes back as a
bare PNG instead of a ZIP. `/mcp/objects/{id}/spritesheet` is a ZIP of one
sheet PNG + layout JSON: one row per animation-direction, uniform cells
sized to the largest frame (nothing resized), `pivot: "cell-center"`.
To get an animation's pixels INLINE, with no download and nothing charged:
`pixelart_workbench(argv=["inspect", "object:<id>:<direction>:<animation>"])`
returns its frames as one sheet image in the tool result. A one-direction
object still needs the direction, and it is the literal `unknown` —
`object:<id>:unknown:<group id>`. `join ref ref --as rows` lays several
animations out one per row (at most 1024 px a side).

include_preview.description: Embed preview image (south for 8-dir, candidates for review).

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__get_portrait_character
tools.description:
Get a portrait ↔ character result by job id.

Returns the sprite (inline + download URL) if completed, or progress/error.

job_id.description: The job id returned by create_portrait_character.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__get_pro_flash_capabilities
tools.description:
Get Pro Flash exact native size pairs, controls and one-image output counts.

Free identity-only lookup. Supply operation, width and height together for
a provisional quote split into image/rotations/total. Finishing a selected
preview bills only rotations; one-direction object finalization costs zero.
Larger research sizes are not supported generation sizes. Read this before
selecting dimensions for image, character or object creation, edit or inpaint.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__get_room
tools.description:
A room's state. While it is being made: its stage and progress. When ready: the room
as painted (inline), its download link and its building kit's (a ZIP of the wall, door
and floor tiles it was built from); once its furniture is cut out
(cut_out_room_furniture), its movable pieces by name and the link that opens it in the
website's room editor (move, remove or bring in pieces; shadows follow).

Download: the room as painted is the `download:` PNG. Its cut-out pieces and its
furniture-free floor are in the `layers:` JSON this prints once the pieces are ready
(public, no auth) — you do not need the editor to export them. Keys: `w`/`h` the
room's pixel size; `room` the painting as you see it; `lit` and `unlit` the SAME room
with every piece removed (the empty floor, lit and unlit); `sprites[]` one entry per
piece with `name`, `x`,`y` (its top-left in those pixels), `foot` (the y of its
LOWEST OPAQUE row, where it stands on the floor — not `y` + the PNG's height,
which may end in transparent rows; sort pieces by it to draw them back to front),
`light`, `img` (a transparent PNG as a data URL), `unlit`, and `shadow` {`x`,`y`,`f`}
as its own PNG at its own position, or null where a piece casts none. An isometric room also has `over`: its low front curbs, which go on
top of the pieces. Every image is a `data:image/png;base64,` URL, so decode it rather
than fetching a second file.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__get_sidescroller_tileset
tools.description:
Get a sidescroller tileset by ID. Returns status, download links, and tile count.
Sidescroller tilesets are for 2D platformer games with transparent backgrounds.

tileset_id.description: ID of the sidescroller tileset to retrieve

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__get_sound_effect
tools.description: Check a sound effect's status and get its audio link (WAV) once it is made.

sound_effect_id.description: A sound_effect_id from create_sound_effect or list_sound_effects

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__get_tiles_pro
tools.description: Get tiles pro by ID. Returns tile data and storage URLs if completed, or progress if processing.

tile_id.description: The UUID of the tiles pro to retrieve. Each returned tile carries the placement rule its sheet uses; the bit meanings are edge/4: bit0=N bit1=E bit2=S bit3=W; a set bit means the painted feature continues across that edge; edge/6: 6 hex edges CCW from vertex 0; a set bit means the OTHER terrain (water) lies beyond that edge; corner/4: NW<<3 | NE<<2 | SW<<1 | SE; a set bit means the first terrain occupies that corner.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__get_topdown_tileset
tools.description:
Get a topdown Wang tileset by ID. Returns status, download links, base tile IDs for chaining, and an example map image.

Download: no auth, the UUID is the key. GET /mcp/tilesets/{id}/image for the sheet PNG (add ?inline=true to be served the bytes instead of a CDN redirect, which Python stdlib clients need; ?layout=wang or ?layout=godot for the website download's Wang or Godot 3x3 arrangement), GET /mcp/tilesets/{id}/metadata for per-tile bounding_box (x/y/width/height, use as atlas regions), corners (NW/NE/SW/SE, each lower/upper/transition, use for Wang autotiling) and pattern_4x4. Both answer 423 + Retry-After while generating. Godot walkthrough: the MCP resource pixellab://docs/godot/wang-tilesets.

tileset_id.description: The UUID of the topdown tileset to retrieve

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__get_ui_asset
tools.description:
Get a UI asset. Processing → progress; completed → image URL + download links.

A template lists the elements split from it (each with its states), or, not
split yet, where update_ui_asset(split=True) would cut it. An element lists its states and
any create_ui_states job still making them. Also the 9-slice, and for a
template a ZIP link with every PNG + metadata.json.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__get_upload_url
tools.description:
Get a URL to upload a local image file to, without needing your API token.

Use it whenever you have an image on disk and a tool wants an image: send
the file with one curl, and pass the `upload:<id>` it returns to any
parameter that takes an image URL (image_urls, reference_image_url,
init_image_url, a style_image "url" ...). This avoids pasting base64 into a
tool call, which clients truncate and can corrupt. Free.

The URL works for 15 minutes and for any number of files. Uploads are kept
3 days. An animated GIF keeps all its frames.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__get_vocal_animation
tools.description:
Check a vocal-animation job and see which mouth positions have landed.

Mouth positions stream in as they are picked, so a running job already
reports partial progress. On completion the set is saved onto the character
and ready for create_talking_gif.

job_id.description: The job id returned by create_vocal_animation.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__image_to_pixelart
tools.description:
Convert an image, render or photo into pixel art.

This is the general-purpose converter: give it any picture and get pixel art
back at the size you ask for. Use it when a user brings their own artwork,
a screenshot, or an AI render and wants it as a sprite.

Two dials decide how much licence the model takes:
- default (faithful=False, init_image_strength=0) — reinterprets the subject
  as pixel art. Cleanest sprites, least like the original.
- faithful=True with init_image_strength around 100-300 — reproduces the
  source. Use it when the user says "keep it exactly like this". Higher is
  NOT more faithful in a useful way: past ~300 the model stops transforming
  and returns the source image, which is not pixel art.

This is the one converter where YOU pick the output size. When the size does
not matter, image_to_pixelart_pro_flash (6 generations) and
image_to_pixelart_pro (20, tier 1+) redraw more cleanly and pick the size from
the picture.

Related tools: create_portrait_character converts a picture into a character
portrait specifically; unzoom_image is what you want if the input is ALREADY
pixel art that has merely been upscaled — running it through here would
redraw art that only needed downscaling.

Input max area 2048x2048, output max 512x512.

Cost: 1 generation. Generation time: ~20-60 seconds (async).
Poll with get_image(job_id).

image_base64.description: Base64 PNG/JPEG of the image to convert. Any artwork, render or photo. PREFER image_url — MCP clients routinely truncate large inline base64.

image_url.description: Alternative to image_base64: an https, data: or `upload:<id>` URL to the source image. PREFER THIS for anything but a tiny sprite. Give one, not both.

output_width.description: Width of the pixel art result. Defaults to a quarter of the source width. Keep the source's aspect ratio.

output_height.description: Height of the pixel art result. Defaults to a quarter of the source height.

faithful.description: Faithful mode. Stays true to the source instead of reinterpreting it as pixel art. Turn this on when the user wants THEIR artwork converted rather than a pixel-art take on it; pair it with a init_image_strength of 100-300.

init_image_strength.description: How strongly to start from the source image (img2img). 0 redraws from scratch using the source only as guidance; 100-300 keeps its composition and colors. Do NOT go higher to be 'more faithful' — past ~300 the model barely transforms the input and hands back the source rather than pixel art.

text_guidance_scale.description: How hard to push towards pixel-art style.

project_id.description: Internal Game Builder project context; the finished image is linked after generation.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__image_to_pixelart_pro
tools.description:
Convert a picture, render or photo into pixel art with the Pro converter —
the strongest redraw of the three converters.

Which converter:
- image_to_pixelart (1 generation): you choose the exact output width and
  height; faithful mode keeps the source's look. Use it when the size matters.
- image_to_pixelart_pro_flash (6 generations): a clean redraw, output size
  picked from the picture. The default when the size does not matter.
- image_to_pixelart_pro (this, 20 generations, tier 1+): the same automatic
  size, the most careful redraw. Use it when pro_flash's result is not good
  enough.
None of them is for art that is already pixel art but upscaled — that only
needs unzoom_image.

The output size is decided by the conversion (the detected pixel scale) and
reported by get_image. For a console or palette look (1-bit, Game Boy, PICO-8,
any palette from Lospec) pass `palette` as its hex colours plus `palette_name`:
every pixel of the result is one of them. Transparent areas of the source
become a white background. Sources over 2048px on the longest side are scaled
down first.

Needs a tier 1 subscription or higher.
Cost: 20 generations at any source size. ~1-3 minutes (async). Poll
get_image(job_id).

image_url.description: An https (or data:) URL to the source picture, or `upload:<id>` (POST /v2/uploads with this same bearer token). PREFER THIS for anything but a tiny image. Give image_url or image_base64, not both.

image_base64.description: Base64 PNG/JPEG of the picture to convert. MCP clients routinely truncate large inline base64 — prefer image_url.

description.description: Optional style notes: 'retro vibes with light dithering', 'sharp edges, muted colours'.

palette.description: Target palette, 2 to 256 hex colours as a JSON array, e.g. ["#081820", "#346856", "#88c070", "#e0f8d0"] for Game Boy or ["#000000", "#ffffff"] for 1-bit. Every pixel the tool draws is one of them; pixels you supplied (a direction you drew) stay as they are.

palette_name.description: Optional name of the palette (e.g. 'Game Boy', 'PICO-8'); naming it helps the look. It only LABELS the colours you pass in palette rather than looking any up, so it cannot be sent on its own.

max_colors.description: At most this many colours (2-64). With a palette, they are picked from it. On the three tools that have a standard mode — create_character, create_topdown_tileset, animate_object — ANY palette setting needs mode='pro': standard refuses palette and max_colors, alone or together. Every other tool taking them has no standard mode and accepts them always.

project_id.description: Internal Game Builder project context; the finished image is linked after generation.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__image_to_pixelart_pro_flash
tools.description:
Convert an image, render or photo into pixel art with Pro Flash.

Redraws the picture as clean pixel art and picks the output size itself
(detected pixel scale), so there is no size parameter. Use image_to_pixelart
instead when the result must be an exact width and height, and
image_to_pixelart_pro (20 generations, tier 1+) when this redraw is not good
enough. Optional
description steers the style (dithering, mood). For a console or palette look
(1-bit, Game Boy, PICO-8, any palette from Lospec) pass `palette` as its hex
colours plus `palette_name`: the picture is drawn for them and every pixel of
the result is one of them.

Supply image_url (preferred), image_base64, or an owned source_image_id.
Sources over 2048px on the longest side are scaled down first. Transparent
areas become a white background.

Cost: 6 generations. ~30-60 seconds. Returns one queued image; poll
get_image(job_id), then download.

palette.description: Target palette, 2 to 256 hex colours as a JSON array, e.g. ["#081820", "#346856", "#88c070", "#e0f8d0"] for Game Boy or ["#000000", "#ffffff"] for 1-bit. Every pixel the tool draws is one of them; pixels you supplied (a direction you drew) stay as they are.

palette_name.description: Optional name of the palette (e.g. 'Game Boy', 'PICO-8'); naming it helps the look. It only LABELS the colours you pass in palette rather than looking any up, so it cannot be sent on its own.

max_colors.description: At most this many colours (2-64). With a palette, they are picked from it. On the three tools that have a standard mode — create_character, create_topdown_tileset, animate_object — ANY palette setting needs mode='pro': standard refuses palette and max_colors, alone or together. Every other tool taking them has no standard mode and accepts them always.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__import_object
tools.description:
Import your own pixel art as a 1-direction object. Free, immediate.

The image becomes a completed object in your library, the same as uploading
it on the website: animate_object, create_object_state, set_canvas_size,
export_asset and place_map_object then work on it like on a generated one.
At most 256x256. Pixels are stored exactly; nothing is regenerated.

image_url.description: URL of the image: https, data:, or upload:<id> from get_upload_url. Preferred over image_base64 for anything but a tiny sprite.

name.description: Object name (optional, max 120 chars).

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__import_tiles
tools.description:
Import your own tiles or tileset sheet (free) — what the website's Import does.

Nothing is generated and nothing is charged. kind='tiles' makes a tile group from
one image per tile (as create_tiles_pro's groups: get_tiles_pro, maps). A tileset
kind cuts one PixelLab-layout sheet into its 16 (or 25) Wang tiles with new base
tile ids, so it chains, maps and downloads like a generated tileset. Sizes are
checked, and a refusal names the size needed.

kind.description: What to make. tiles: a tile group (get_tiles_pro), one image per tile. topdown_tileset / sidescroller_tileset: a Wang tileset (get_topdown_tileset / get_sidescroller_tileset) from ONE sheet.

images.description: JSON array of image references: an https URL, upload:<id>, gallery:<id>, job:<id>[:<index>], a data URL or base64 PNG. kind='tiles': one per tile, 1-32. A tileset kind: exactly one sheet in PixelLab's layout - the 15-tileset sheet a tileset download gives (4x4 tiles, 4x8 for a tall set) or the 8-wide native sheet.

tile_size.description: kind='tiles': required, the tile size in pixels (the images' width; square_topdown and octagon tiles are tile_size square). Tilesets: 16, 24, 32 or 64, read from the sheet when omitted; give it when a size reads two ways (256x256 is a 64px 4x4 or a 32px 8-wide sheet).

description.description: kind='tiles': what the tiles are (default 'Imported tiles').

tile_view.description: kind='tiles': the view they are drawn in (default low top-down).

tile_view_angle.description: kind='tiles': view angle in degrees, if known.

lower_description.description: Tilesets: the lower terrain (sidescroller: the platform).

transition_description.description: Tilesets: the strip between the terrains.

name.description: Tilesets: display name (default: cropped from the descriptions).

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__improve_music_style
tools.description:
Write a short music idea out as a full style for create_music.

Returns a sentence or two that gives each instrument a role, the mood and the
ending: edit it if you like, then pass it as create_music's style (with the same
instrumental and bpm).

Cost: 0.05 generations, or about $0.002 in credits. Synchronous, ~5-15 seconds.

style.description: A short idea: 'spooky swamp level', 'cozy farming village'.

instrumental.description: Whether the song will be instrumental.

bpm.description: The tempo you will send to create_music, for the text to keep.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__inpaint_image
tools.description:
Regenerate one region of an image, keeping everything else pixel-identical.

This is the repair tool: fix a malformed hand, erase a stray pixel cluster,
swap just the cape, add an item to a specific spot. The area outside the
mask is frozen, so the rest of the sprite cannot drift.

Give the area as a rectangle (easiest — you only need coordinates):
  inpaint_image(image_base64=<png>, description="a clean open hand",
                mask_x=18, mask_y=30, mask_width=14, mask_height=14)
or supply your own mask (white = regenerate, black = keep):
  inpaint_image(image_base64=<png>, description="...", mask_image_base64=<png>)

Related: edit_image rewrites the WHOLE image from an instruction (no mask);
create_map_object generates a new object matching a background's style and
returns a transparent cutout, not your edited image.

Image must be 32x32-512x512; above 256px on a side needs a Tier 2 plan.
Cost: 10 generations for any SQUARE canvas up to 256x256 (so 64x64 and 88x88
are both 10), 15 up to 341x341, 25 above. The whole image sets the price, not
the mask. A NON-SQUARE canvas is measured against the nearest of ten aspect
ratios, so BOTH sides count and neither the longest side nor the area decides
it. The 10 ceiling then the 15 ceiling, by ratio: 1:1 256x256 then 341x341 |
5:4 288x232 then 384x309 | 4:3 300x224 then 400x298 | 3:2 316x212 then
421x282 | 16:9 344x192 then 458x256 | 21:9 396x168 then 528x224 (that last
one is past this tool's own 512px side limit, so it is unreachable); a portrait
canvas takes its own ratio's pair swapped (4:5, 3:4, 2:3, 9:16, and anything
taller than 9:16 snaps to 9:16). A canvas fitting inside a ceiling costs that
band and anything past the second one is 25, so 360x168 is 10 and 168x360 is
15, and 220x256 is 10 where 220x400 is 15 and 220x512 is 25.
Generation time: ~30-90 seconds (async).
Poll with get_image(job_id).

description.description: What should appear in the masked area (e.g. 'a clean four-finger hand holding a sword', 'plain grass, no object').

image_base64.description: Base64 PNG to repair. 32x32 to 512x512. Everything outside the mask is preserved exactly. PREFER image_url — MCP clients routinely truncate large inline base64, which corrupts the image.

image_url.description: Alternative to image_base64: an https, data: or `upload:<id>` URL to the PNG to repair. PREFER THIS for anything but a tiny sprite — inline base64 is often cut off mid-string by MCP clients. Give one, not both.

mask_x.description: Left edge of the rectangular area to regenerate.

mask_y.description: Top edge of the rectangular area to regenerate.

mask_width.description: Width of the area to regenerate.

mask_height.description: Height of the area to regenerate.

mask_image_base64.description: Custom mask, same size as the image: WHITE = regenerate, BLACK = keep. Use instead of mask_x/y/width/height when the area isn't a rectangle. A greyscale (mode L) PNG is accepted and converted, but keep it pure 0/255 — white and black are the only values with a defined meaning. The size must match exactly; masks are never rescaled.

mask_image_url.description: Alternative to mask_image_base64: an https, data: or `upload:<id>` URL to the mask PNG. Give one, not both.

crop_to_mask.description: Confine generated content to the mask boundary for clean edges.

no_background.description: Background handling. Default (unset) follows the input: a sprite with transparency stays transparent, an opaque image stays opaque. Pass False to flatten a transparent input onto white.

project_id.description: Internal Game Builder project context; the finished image is linked after generation.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__inpaint_image_pro_flash
tools.description:
Replace white-mask pixels with Pro Flash, preserving unmasked RGBA bytes exactly.

Source: image_url, image_base64, or owned source_image_id. Mask: a rectangle
(all four mask_x/y/width/height), OR a same-size mask PNG via base64/URL.
Mask RGB must be pure white=generate or black=keep; mask alpha is ignored.
Empty masks are rejected. crop_to_mask is always true. Changes-only output
is transparent outside the mask; Modify current layer returns a composite.
Optional context_image requires bounding_box locating the source and is at
most three times its native dimensions. No images or masks are rescaled.
Query get_pro_flash_capabilities for shapes; poll the job with get_image.

Cost: by the SOURCE canvas's longest side, not the mask — 5 generations up to
96px, 6 from 100 to 208, 9 from 212 to 256, for one image. So a 64x64 repair
is 5 and 128x64 is 6, against inpaint_image's 10 for either. Shrinking the
mask does not lower it. get_pro_flash_capabilities(operation="inpaint",
width=, height=) prices an exact size for free.

mask_image_base64.description: Mask PNG, exactly the source size. EVERY pixel's RGB must be pure white (generate) or pure black (keep): a grey or coloured pixel is refused, so remove any antialiasing, and a mask with no white at all is refused too. The mask's own alpha is ignored. Unlike inpaint_image, which does not check this, Pro Flash enforces it. Or give the four mask_x/y/width/height instead.

mask_image_url.description: Same mask as mask_image_base64, from an https, data: or `upload:<id>` URL.

context_image.description: The surrounding scene to match, not a style reference. Pass it WITH bounding_box or not at all. At most 3x the source canvas in each dimension and never rescaled. Exactly ONE of its three sources.

usage_description.description: How this reference should guide appearance.

bounding_box.description: Where the source canvas sits inside context_image: width/height must equal the source size, and the box must lie entirely within the context image.

no_background.description: Background removal on the GENERATED pixels. Left out it follows the source: on if the source has any non-opaque pixel, off if it is fully opaque. Removal runs before the frozen pixels are copied back, so masked pixels CAN come back transparent (how a bigger hairstyle keeps gaps around it) and pixels outside the mask are untouched either way. Off, the render is drawn on a background, so the masked area comes back opaque.

output_method.description: What comes back, always at the source's own size. `Modify current layer` (default) is the whole sprite with the mask area replaced. `Modify current layer, only changes` and `New layer with changes` are that same canvas holding ONLY the masked pixels, fully transparent everywhere else - a layer to drop over your own art. Every pixel outside the mask is copied from your source byte for byte, and that copy is the LAST step, after background removal and palette work, so nothing outside the mask can shift.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__inpaint_map
tools.description:
Regenerate one rectangular area of a map with AI — a ramp, a broken wall, a
path through a forest, a seam between two terrains — the way Map Workshop's
inpainting does. Give the area in the same cells get_map and edit_map use.

Choosing the area: put what you want near its centre and make it a bit
larger than that, with a cell or two of the map you keep on every side. The
model blends the new pixels into what it sees at the area's edges; something
that runs into an edge (a stream, a wall) can end in a visible step where the
area stops.

The new pixels go into the map's inpainted layer, which sits over the
terrain and under objects, exactly where Map Workshop puts its own
inpainting; the terrain cells underneath are unchanged.

Cost: like inpaint_image_pro_flash, by the area's longest side in pixels — 5
generations up to 96px, 6 up to 208px, 9 up to 256px. Not available on
sidescroller maps or maps with tile layers (the area could not be drawn here
as Map Workshop shows it).

Non-blocking: returns a job_id. Poll inpaint_map(map_id=..., job_id=...);
when the job completes the result is written into the map (also
automatically) and the poll shows the area.

description.description: What the area should become, e.g. 'a wooden ramp from the shore up to the dock'. The model sees the map around it and continues its terrain, perspective and palette.

x.description: Area: left edge, in terrain cells

y.description: Area: top edge, in terrain cells

width.description: Area width in cells. 32-256px per side in multiples of 4px: 2-16 cells on a 16px map, 1-8 on a 32px map.

height.description: Area height in cells, as width

no_background.description: Keep only the new subject: its background is removed, so the terrain under the area shows through around it. Default False replaces the whole area, as Map Workshop does by default.

job_id.description: Poll an earlier inpaint_map call instead of starting one: reports progress, and once it is done makes sure the result is in the map and shows the area. Pass with map_id only.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__list_characters
tools.description:
List your characters with status. Returns compact one-line-per-character format.
Use get_character(character_id) for full details on any character.

limit.description: Maximum number of characters to return

tags.description: Comma-separated tags to filter by (ANY match). Example: 'wizard,fire'

search.description: Filter by name, case-insensitive. Matches the name shown here and the description it was created from, so 'wizard' finds 'old wizard with a staff'.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__list_images
tools.description:
List the images in your Creator gallery (pixellab.ai/create), newest first,
one line each: its `gallery:<id>` reference, description, size and frame
count. Pass the reference to get_image to download an image, to
pixelart_workbench to look at or edit it, and to save_to_asset to save a fix
over it.

limit.description: Maximum number of images to return

search.description: Filter by the description an image was made from, or its id, case-insensitive. 'knight' finds 'armored knight with a sword'.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__list_isometric_tiles
tools.description:
List your isometric tiles. One line per tile with status.
Use get_isometric_tile(tile_id) for full details.

limit.description: Maximum number of tiles to return

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__list_jobs
tools.description:
List your active background jobs (pending + processing).

Use this to find stuck jobs you can cancel with cancel_job.

include_recent.description: Include recently completed/failed jobs (last 30 min). Default: only active jobs.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__list_map_objects
tools.description:
List the objects and characters placed on a map, with their cell positions.

Gives you the placement id that move_map_object and remove_map_object take.
A placement id is per-PLACEMENT, not per-asset — the same tree placed twice
has two ids.

limit.description: Max rows to return

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__list_maps
tools.description:
List your maps, most recently edited first.

Pass `search` to find one by name — accounts reach four figures of maps, so
paging is not a way to look something up. Maps are made in PixelLab's Map
Workshop; use get_map to see one and edit_map to paint terrain on it.

limit.description: How many maps to return

search.description: Only maps whose name contains this (case-insensitive)

offset.description: Skip this many, to page deeper

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__list_music
tools.description:
List your songs and loops, newest first: id | name | status | length | kind.

Being made, failed and finished songs, the two takes of a request side by side.
Use get_music(song_id) for one song's audio and details.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__list_objects
tools.description:
List your objects with status and progress. One line per object.
Use get_object(object_id) for full details.

tags.description: Comma-separated tags to filter by (matches ANY tag).

status_filter.description: Filter by status: completed, review, pending, processing, failed, expanding, review-expansion (an 8-direction expansion running, then waiting to be kept or discarded).

search.description: Filter by name, case-insensitive. Matches the name shown here and the description it was created from, so 'chest' finds 'treasure chest'.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__list_projects
tools.description: List your projects with IDs: game projects (with branches and git clone URLs) and folders, which only group assets on the website. add_to_project files assets into either; manage_project makes, renames or deletes a folder.

kind.description: 'game' for game projects only, 'folder' for folders only, 'all' both

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__list_rooms
tools.description:
List your rooms (made with create_room), newest first: id, status, view, name and
doors. get_room(room_id) gives one room's picture, door anchors and walkable rects.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__list_sidescroller_tilesets
tools.description:
List your sidescroller (platformer) tilesets. One line per tileset with status.
Use get_sidescroller_tileset(tileset_id) for full details.

limit.description: Maximum number of tilesets to return

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__list_sound_effects
tools.description:
List your sound effects, newest first: id | name | status | length.

Being made, failed and finished ones. Use get_sound_effect(sound_effect_id) for
one clip's audio and prompt.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__list_tiles_pro
tools.description:
List your tiles (pro). One line per tile with status.
Use get_tiles_pro(tile_id) for full details.

limit.description: Maximum number of tiles to return

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__list_topdown_tilesets
tools.description:
List your top-down Wang tilesets. One line per tileset with status.
Use get_topdown_tileset(tileset_id) for full details.

limit.description: Maximum number of tilesets to return

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__list_ui_assets
tools.description:
List your UI panels with status. One line per asset.
Use get_ui_asset(ui_asset_id) for full details.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__make_music_loop
tools.description:
Make one of your songs into game music that loops seamlessly.

The song is made again so that the part between its intro and its ending
repeats without a seam: two new takes, each with loop points. Play the take to
loop_end, then jump back to loop_start (get_music shows both, in seconds). The
intro plays once, the ending never. Instrumental songs only, for now.

Cost: 4 generations, or $0.033 in credits; charged once the takes are made.
Needs a tier 2 subscription or higher.

Generation time: ~1.5-2.5 minutes (async). Poll with get_music or wait_for_jobs.

song_id.description: A finished instrumental song of yours (create_music, list_music); not a loop.

project_id.description: Internal Game Builder project context; the finished loop is linked after generation.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__manage_project
tools.description:
Manage your projects (list_projects shows them). A folder only groups your assets on
the website: no workspace, git repo or deploy; file assets into it with
add_to_project. Renaming keeps a game's address. Deleting a folder keeps its assets
(they go back to "No project"); game projects are deleted on the website only.
Rename and delete are for organization admins.

action.description: create_folder: make a folder (needs name). rename: rename a game project or folder (needs project_id and name). delete_folder: delete a folder (needs project_id); its assets are kept.

project_id.description: For rename / delete_folder: a project from list_projects. Leave out for create_folder.

name.description: For create_folder / rename: the name.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__manage_state
tools.description:
Copy a character or object state, or split it off into an asset of its own. Free.

duplicate: the copy gets the rotations, tags and project links, not the
animations, and is named after the source ('Idle (copy)', 'Idle (copy 2)'). Use
it to keep the original before editing a state with save_to_asset or
set_canvas_size. The source must be completed.

ungroup: the state keeps its id, own name, rotations and animations; the new
asset is named after the old one with the next copy number. A character/object
with one state has nothing to split off.

asset_id.description: Id of the character or object state.

action.description: duplicate: copy the state into a new state of the same asset. ungroup: remove the state from its character/object, making it an asset of its own.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__mirror_animation
tools.description:
Create an animation's missing opposite direction by flipping one horizontally. Free, immediate.

The flipped frames are added to the same animation (same animation_group_id)
as the opposite direction. Refused when that direction already exists:
delete it first with delete_animation(direction=...) to replace it. South and
north cannot be mirrored. Faster and free compared with generating the
direction, and exact for symmetric sprites; asymmetric details (a sword in
the right hand) end up in the other hand.

asset_id.description: Id of the character or object.

source_direction.description: Direction to flip. Creates its mirror: east <-> west, south-east <-> south-west, north-east <-> north-west.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__move_map_object
tools.description:
Move a placed object or character to a different cell or an exact pixel, or
change its layer.

Keeps its sprite and refs. world_x/world_y positions it to the pixel, as Map
Workshop's free drag does; `layer` alone re-orders it without moving it.

x.description: Cell to stand it on, as in get_map

y.description: Cell to stand it on, as in get_map

world_x.description: Exact position in world pixels, instead of x/y

anchor.description: What world_x/world_y name: 'foot' (default) = the sprite's bottom-centre; 'top_left' = the box origin, box_px in list_map_objects

layer.description: New draw order (higher is on top). Pass it alone to change only the layer: the stored position, fractions included, is untouched.

show.description: Return a rendered image of the result

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__pixelart_workbench
tools.description:
Run one pixel-art command on a drawing or image you already made. This is
the engine's own command line: it checks work, explains it and improves it.

Commands: check and explain (read-only):
- lint <id> [--rules outline_gap,orphan_pixel,...] — pixel-art defects, each
  naming the node and command that drew them
- inspect <id> --region x0,y0,x1,y1 --scale 10 — a zoomed crop with its
  exact colours, to LOOK at: the id it returns still holds the whole
  picture, so passing it on sends the full canvas and not the region.
  `split ... --count` below is what actually cuts a piece out
- measure <id> --at x,y — what is at a pixel and who drew it
- explain <id> — resolved geometry, per-command footprints, before rendering
- motion / storyboard / silhouette / reveal / clusters / parts <id> — reports
- score <id> — a 0-100 pixel-art discipline score with a breakdown
- compare <id> <id> — two results side by side
Improve (returns a NEW drawing id):
- shade <id> --band 2 --light=-1,-1 — banded shading along a colour ramp
- selout <id> — selective outlining; reoutline / clean-lines / aa / mirror
- cluster <id> --at x,y --action recolor --color <name> — one guarded cluster
- repair <id> — deterministic cleanup of drift, strays, fringe and noise
Sheets and frames (returns a NEW image id):
- split <image> --grid 3x3 [--count n] — a sprite sheet, strip or grid as an
  animation, one frame per cell (columns x rows). --count keeps the first n
  cells and drops the rest, so `split <image> --grid 2x1 --count 1` is the
  free exact crop of the left half, `--grid 1x2 --count 1` the top half, and
  a one-cell result downloads as image.png (a multi-frame one has no
  image.png, only frames.png — which is why a plain 2x1 split cannot be
  handed on as a single picture). Cells must divide the canvas evenly; the
  error names the counts that fit. Without --count, trailing cells that are
  one flat colour are dropped
- join <image> <image> ... [--as sheet|rows|animation] [--columns n] — pictures
  or animations as one sprite sheet, one per row, or one animation
- scale <image> --by 4 — the same picture or animation bigger, each pixel a
  4x4 block (a sticker, a print); nothing is redrawn
A result comes back as an image in the reply AND as a no-auth URL the reply
prints, `/mcp/pixel-tools/<id>/image.png` (`frames.png` for the frames of a
multi-frame one) — so a sheet you joined is both readable inline and
downloadable. Sheets hold at most 1024 px a side; `join` refuses a larger
one rather than shrinking the art, and says how many frames do fit.
Craft operations need colour ramps: run `extract-palette <id>` first, then
pass `--ramps skin=dark,mid,light`.
Authoring: `edit <id> --changes '[...]'` applies exact pixel operations and
`draw <id> --recipe '{...}'` builds or revises a layered scene; both take JSON
whose fields are NOT listed here. Colours in that JSON are always `#RRGGBB`
or `#RRGGBBAA` with alpha `00` or `ff` — `rgb()` and bare hex are refused,
and nothing strips the `#`, since argv is a JSON list rather than a shell
line. Every `edit` change carries `operation`, `layer`, `frames` (ONE-based)
and `reason`; coordinates are zero-based and a `region` is `[x0,y0,x1,y1]`
inclusive. Then its own fields: `patch_pixels` takes `pixels`, a list of
`[x,y,expected,replacement]` (1-10000, each assigned only where the pixel
already holds `expected`, so a mismatch fails the pass); `copy_region` takes
`source_layer`, `source_frame`, `region`, `at` `[x,y]`; `map_colors` takes
`region` and `colors` `{"#from":"#to"}` (alpha must match); `flood_fill`
`seed`/`expected`/`color`; `brush` `points` plus `color`; `outline` `mode`
(outside|inside|recolor|erase). The full contracts and any command's flags
are one free call away: `describe edits | paint | outline | draw | animation
| motion | scenes | review`, `<command> -h`, `describe cli`.
Free for subscribers.

argv.description: One command line, e.g. 'lint <drawing_id> --rules outline_gap' or ['edit', '<id>', '--changes', '[...]']. Omit it for the playbook. A subject is an id or an image reference — never a file path; the server writes the output and returns a new id. A reference is `character:<id>:<direction>` for a rotation, `character:<id>:<direction>:<animation>` for every frame of that animation (the display name, type or [group: ...] id get_character prints), the same two forms for `object:<id>` (a one-direction object's direction is the literal `unknown`), `gallery:<id>`, `job:<id>`, `upload:<id>`, a data URL, an https link or base64. That is how a stored animation's pixels come back inline without downloading anything. Start with 'describe cli' for the full command list.

mode.description: low (default): act directly, fewest tokens — one decisive image per result. high: think openly — fuller evidence and a review checklist; write your plan and observations in `notes`. Use the mode the user asked for.

notes.description: What you observed and what this step should achieve, in a few sentences (high mode: always; low: optional). On the first call, include the user's request. Stored with the step to improve these tools.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__place_map_object
tools.description:
Place objects or characters on a map, at a terrain cell or an exact pixel.

Objects are how a map gets trees, houses, rocks and NPCs — terrain painting
(edit_map) only covers ground. A tileset tiles a SURFACE, so anything with a
silhouette has to be an object.

Position: x/y stands the sprite on that cell (the coordinates get_map
shows). world_x/world_y puts it at an exact world pixel instead, as Map
Workshop's free drag does — use it to match positions from a game scene or
an isometric layout that does not fall on the cell grid.

For many objects pass `placements`: one call, one save.

Returns a picture of the result by default, because a placement that is one
cell off, or far bigger than you expected, is invisible in text.

x.description: Terrain cell to stand the object on, as in get_map

y.description: Terrain cell to stand the object on, as in get_map

world_x.description: Exact position in world pixels, instead of x/y — the space of the map's object boundingBox and the game's sprites

anchor.description: What world_x/world_y name: 'foot' (default) = the sprite's bottom-centre; 'top_left' = the box origin, box_px in list_map_objects

character_id.description: Character UUID from list_characters

direction.description: Facing for a character (south, north, east...). Leave unset for objects — most have a single sprite and it is picked automatically.

layer.description: Draw order; higher is on top. Defaults to the next layer.

placements.description: Place many in one call, instead of the single-placement arguments: [{"object_id":"...","x":3,"y":4}, {"object_id":"...","world_x":412,"world_y":230,"anchor":"foot"}, {"character_id":"...","x":1,"y":1,"direction":"south"}]. Each item takes the same fields as above. One save for all; if any item is invalid nothing is placed.

character_id.description: Character UUID from list_characters

x.description: Terrain cell to stand it on

y.description: Terrain cell to stand it on

anchor.description: What world_x/world_y name: 'foot' (bottom-centre, default) or 'top_left' (the stored box origin, box_px in list_map_objects)

layer.description: Draw order; higher is on top

show.description: Return a rendered image of the placement

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__place_map_tiles
tools.description:
Place, stack and erase tiles on a map's tile layers — the map editor's tile
painting, with its Stack layer control.

A map made from tile groups (isometric, hex, oblique, square tiles) keeps
each group as a tile layer; get_map lists them and shows, per cell, the
tile on top and its stack level. A cell holds a column of tiles: level 0
is the ground, and each level above sits one tile height higher, so a
`stack` of 3 builds a pillar and "on_top" builds on whatever is there.

Placing on a cell's level replaces the tile already there. As in the
editor, a tile placed on one ground layer clears that same cell and level
on any other ground layer drawn on the same grid.

Tiles go down exactly as given: for connected sets, pick the tile drawn
for that spot's neighbours (get_tiles_pro lists each tile's mask).

A building kit is several layers: floor, interior walls, outer walls, roof
(when the kit has roof pieces) and pieces (pillars, doorways, stairs). Lay
floor tiles and the outer walls follow the floor's outline. Interior walls
and roofs take no tile: each cell's piece follows its neighbours. A doorway
is cut into the wall at that cell, and stairs lay both halves. get_map lists
what each kit layer takes.

Returns what changed and a view of the area: the top tile and the top
level of every cell, and each stacked column level by level.

oneOf.description: Put one tile on cells, `stack` levels high.

layer.description: Tile layer index, as listed by get_map

area.description: An inclusive block of cells: q..q+width-1, r..r+height-1.

tile.description: Tile index in the layer's tile group. Left out on a building kit's interior-wall and roof layers, whose pieces follow their neighbours

oneOf.description: Remove tiles: everything from `level` up, or the top `stack` with on_top.

layer.description: Tile layer index, as listed by get_map

area.description: An inclusive block of cells: q..q+width-1, r..r+height-1.

oneOf.description: Lay another tile group on the map as new layers, after the existing ones.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__reduce_colors
tools.description:
Quantize images onto a smaller, shared palette.

Pixel art reads as pixel art partly because of its restricted palette. AI
output and converted artwork often carry hundreds of near-identical colors;
this snaps them onto a tight palette, optionally with ordered dithering.

Passing several frames in one call is the point: they are quantized TOGETHER,
so an animation or a character's eight directions come back sharing ONE
palette instead of drifting apart frame by frame. Quantizing them one at a
time is the mistake this tool exists to prevent.

Three ways to choose the palette:
- omit num_colors and the palette image — the size is auto-detected
- num_colors — quantize to exactly this many colors
- palette_image — reuse the colors of an existing image (the game's palette)

The result carries a `palette` strip you can feed back as palette_image_base64
to lock later frames onto the same colors.

Total size limit across all frames is 512x512 worth of pixels (sixteen 64x64
frames, or four 128x128).

Cost: 0.1 generations. Runs locally in about a second — poll once with
get_image(job_id).

images_base64.description: Base64 PNG(s) to quantize — pass a one-element list for a single image. All frames must be the same size. PREFER image_urls; MCP clients routinely truncate large inline base64.

image_urls.description: Alternative to images_base64: https, data: or `upload:<id>` (POST /v2/uploads with this same bearer token) URLs to the PNG(s), one per frame. PREFER THIS. Give urls OR base64, not both.

num_colors.description: Target number of colors. Omit to auto-detect a good palette size from the images. Cannot be combined with a palette image.

palette_image_base64.description: Base64 PNG whose colors become the palette (max 256 colors) — use it to force frames onto an existing game palette. Cannot be combined with num_colors.

palette_image_url.description: Alternative to palette_image_base64: an https, data: or `upload:<id>` URL to the palette image. Give one, not both.

dithering.description: Ordered dithering matrix size. Larger matrices give smoother gradients at the cost of a busier look.

dithering_strength.description: How strongly to dither. Ignored when dithering is 'none'.

project_id.description: Internal Game Builder project context; the finished image is linked after generation.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__remove_background
tools.description:
Remove the background from an image you already have, leaving the subject on
transparency. Same size in and out.

The generators' no_background=True only applies while they draw. Use this for
an image that already exists: one from the gallery or another tool that came
back on a backdrop, an uploaded sprite sheet frame, a screenshot, a picture a
user brought.

Max 400x400 in area (e.g. 400x400, 200x800). One image per call.

Cost: 1 generation. Usually ~10-30 seconds (async). Poll get_image(job_id).

image.description: The image to cut out: `gallery:<id>`, `job:<id>` or `job:<id>:<index>` (an image tool result), `character:<id>:<direction>`, `object:<id>[:<direction>]`, `upload:<id>`, a pixelart_workbench result id, an https or data URL of a PNG, or base64. One frame: an animation is cut out one call per frame. Prefer a reference or URL to inline base64.

background_removal_task.description: remove_simple_background (default): faster, for a flat or simple backdrop. remove_complex_background: slower, for a detailed scene behind the subject or fiddly edges.

description.description: Optional: what the foreground subject is ('a knight with a spear'), so the right thing is kept.

project_id.description: Internal Game Builder project context; the finished image is linked after generation.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__remove_from_project
tools.description:
Stop a game project from using a character, object, tileset, map, room, UI
asset, song or sound effect, or take an asset out of a folder (or a tile group
or isometric tile out of the game it is filed under).

This unlinks the art from the project. It does NOT delete the art: the
asset stays in your library and can be added back at any time, and any
other project using it is untouched. Use delete_character / delete_object /
delete_topdown_tileset / delete_map / delete_room to actually destroy something.

Until now add_to_project had no inverse, so a project could accumulate art
it no longer used — and a map that fails to export blocks every deploy of
that project, with no way back out.

The kind is worked out from the id; you do not have to say which it is.
Calling twice is harmless.

project_id.description: The game project or folder, from list_projects

asset_id.description: A character, object, tileset, map, room, UI asset, tile group, isometric tile, image, song, sound effect or audio file currently in the project — the id you passed to add_to_project

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__remove_map_object
tools.description:
Remove placed objects or characters from a map.

Deletes placements only — the object or character itself is untouched and can
be placed again. Pass `placement_id` for one, or `asset_id` to clear every
placement of one asset at once.

asset_id.description: Remove EVERY placement of this object or character instead — the asset_id column in list_map_objects. Use it to clear one prop from a whole map in a single call.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__rename_asset
tools.description:
Rename a character, object, tileset, map or UI asset, or one animation. Free, immediate.

Characters and objects carry two names: `name` is the asset's (what
list_characters / list_objects show, shared by every state) and
`state_name` is this state's own. Pass either or both. Characters also take
`description`, the text later animations and states are made from.

For an animation, pass the character/object id, its `animation_group_id`
and the new `name`; every direction of it is renamed.

asset_id.description: Id of your character, object, tileset, map or UI asset (from its list_* or get_* tool).

name.description: New name (max 120 characters). For a character/object this is the asset's name, shared by all its states. With animation_group_id it names that animation.

state_name.description: Characters/objects only: new name for this one state (e.g. 'Idle', 'armored').

description.description: Characters only: new character description. Animations and states made afterwards use it; existing art is unchanged.

animation_group_id.description: Rename one animation of the character/object instead: its [group: ...] id from get_character/get_object. Put the new name in `name`.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__rename_music
tools.description: Rename one of your songs, in your library and in the games it is in.

song_id.description: A song_id from create_music or list_music

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__rename_sound_effect
tools.description: Rename one of your sound effects, in your library and in the games it is in.

sound_effect_id.description: A sound_effect_id from create_sound_effect or list_sound_effects

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__sandbox_bash
tools.description: Run a shell command in the sandbox (/workspace). Available: node, npm, git, tsc, and `wrangler deploy` — builds + deploys the game's unified Cloudflare Worker (frontend + /api + multiplayer /room -> {slug}.pixellab.run) and runs a smoke test. Use `wrangler deploy` to deploy (there is no separate deploy tool); `wrangler tail` shows the worker's runtime logs. Don't run build.sh / npm build directly — wrangler deploy builds.

timeout.description: Seconds before the command is killed. Default 300; a command that runs `wrangler deploy` gets at least 1200 (a build on a large asset library takes minutes).

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__sandbox_create_session
tools.description: Create a sandbox session for a game project. Returns session_id + file tree + git log. Working directory: /workspace. Tools: Node.js 20, npm, git, tsc. Session expires after 30 min idle.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__sandbox_deploy_worker
tools.description: Build and deploy a Cloudflare Worker for a chat project. Deploys the unified Worker (frontend + /api + multiplayer /room) to {project_slug}.pixellab.run. Requires an active sandbox session.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__sandbox_destroy_session
tools.description: Destroy a sandbox session. Syncs to storage by default.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__sandbox_edit
tools.description: Edit a file via search-and-replace. old_string must match exactly once.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__sandbox_playtest
tools.description: Playtest a deployed game using a vision AI subagent. The subagent opens the game in a browser, takes screenshots, and interacts via keyboard/mouse following your instruction. Returns a text report of observations. Takes 30-60s. Cost: ~1 generation, usually less.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__sandbox_read
tools.description: Read a file from the sandbox. Returns content with line numbers.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__sandbox_read_image
tools.description: Read an image file from the sandbox and analyze it with a vision model. Returns a text description of the image contents. Cost: ~1 generation, usually less.

path.description: Path to the image file in the sandbox (e.g. 'game/assets/player.png').

question.description: What to analyze about the image — be specific (e.g. 'Is the player sprite facing south?', 'What colors are used in this tileset?').

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__sandbox_run
tools.description:
Code Mode: run a JavaScript snippet in the project sandbox (Node, cwd /workspace) to do many file/shell ops in ONE call instead of chaining sandbox_read/write/edit/bash. Your code is an async function body with a typed `sandbox` API + console.log:
  sandbox.read(path)->string · sandbox.write(path,content) · sandbox.edit(path,old,new) (errors if old not found) · sandbox.ls(dir?)->string[] · sandbox.sh(cmd)->stdout
`return` a value to report it. Example: `const p=JSON.parse(sandbox.read('website/package.json')); console.log(p.name); return sandbox.ls('website/src');`  Returns console output + the returned value (or the error). Use `sandbox.sh('wrangler deploy')` to deploy.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__sandbox_sync
tools.description: Save current git state to persistent storage.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__sandbox_undeploy
tools.description: Remove deployed files from S3 and invalidate CloudFront cache for a project branch. Use after deleting a project or to clean up a stale preview deployment.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__sandbox_write
tools.description: Create or overwrite a file in the sandbox. Creates parent directories automatically.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__save_to_asset
tools.description:
Save pixel art into one of your characters, objects, Creator gallery
images or tilesets, replacing a rotation, one direction of an animation, a
gallery image or a tileset's tiles — or add it to the gallery as a new image
(free, no generation).

Use it to keep a fix made with pixelart_workbench or another image tool: the
character and object creators, the Creator gallery, the map editor, downloads
and game projects then show the new pixels. The image must match what it replaces —
the same canvas size and the same number of frames; a different size can go
to the gallery as a new image. Save each direction with its own call. The
replaced frames are kept: the reply gives the save_to_asset call that puts
them back.

Examples:
- save_to_asset(image="<workbench id>", target="character:<id>:south")
- save_to_asset(image="<workbench id>", target="character:<id>:east:<group id>")
- save_to_asset(image="<workbench id>", target="object:<id>")
- save_to_asset(image="<workbench id>", target="gallery:<id>")
- save_to_asset(image="<workbench id>", target="gallery:new",
  description="knight holding a sword, idle")
- save_to_asset(image="<edited sheet>", target="tileset:<id>")

image.description: What to save: a pixelart_workbench result id (`<id>`, or `<id>:<view>` for a drawing), `job:<id>` / `job:<id>:<index>` (an image tool result), `upload:<id>` (an image POSTed to /v2/uploads), an https or data URL of a PNG or GIF, or base64. A PNG is one frame, even a strip: an animation's frames go as a GIF (one duration for all), a multi-image `job:<id>` or a multi-frame pixelart_workbench result.

target.description: Where to save it. A rotation: `character:<id>:<direction>`, `object:<id>:<direction>`, or `object:<id>` for a one-direction object. One direction of an animation: the same with `:<group id>` added (get_character / get_object show each animation's [group: ...] id). A Creator gallery image: `gallery:<id>` to replace it (list_images shows each image's reference), `gallery:new` to add the image as a new one. A top-down or sidescroller tileset: `tileset:<id>` with its whole sheet (the download_png layout, same size), keeping its id and tile layout.

description.description: Only with target="gallery:new": what the image shows, kept as its gallery description so the website and list_images(search=...) can find it.

name.description: Only with target="gallery:new": the image's name, as the website's Rename sets it. Without one, a game project shows the description's first 60 characters, so give distinct names to images whose descriptions start alike.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__search_help

question.description: What you need help with (tools, workflows, billing, features, deployment). Include the context you are working in. Max 2000 characters.

tool.description: A tool's name, e.g. 'animate_character': returns its full reference (every option, price and limit) as written, at once and free. Pass instead of question.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__search_knowledge
tools.description:
Search the Phaser/game dev knowledge base for tips, patterns, and code examples.

Returns semantically matched tips from the curated knowledge base — useful
for Phaser 4 patterns, TypeScript game dev, Vite build issues, map systems,
collision, camera follow, and other game builder topics.

query.description: Search query — describe the Phaser/TypeScript/game dev topic you need help with (e.g. 'camera follow player', 'collision detection', 'map transitions').

limit.description: Max results to return.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__select_object_frames
tools.description:
Promote selected frames of a review object to individual completed objects.

See get_object on a review-status object to view candidates inline.
Each selected index becomes its own 1-direction object. Once no frames
remain in the review object it is deleted automatically. If a call times
out it may still finish: check get_object before retrying (promoted frames
leave the review object, and re-selecting one is refused).

On an 8-direction expansion review (expand_object_to_8_directions, status
review-expansion), call it with no indices to keep the expansion: the same
object becomes 8-direction, its canvas grows to the review's size and its
animations move to the expansion's existing direction.

indices.description: 0-based indices of frames to keep. Each becomes a separate completed 1-direction object. Leave out on an 8-direction expansion review (status review-expansion): that keeps all 8 directions.

common_tag.description: Optional tag applied to every newly-created object.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__set_canvas_size
tools.description:
Change a character's or object's canvas size by adding or removing transparent margin. Free.

Every rotation is re-centred on the new canvas about its pivot. The art is
never scaled or cropped: a size smaller than the art itself is refused with
the art's bounds. Animations keep the canvas they were made on; an object's
map placements follow it. Use it to give a sprite room before animating
(a sword swing, a jump) or to trim empty margin.

asset_id.description: Id of the character or object.

width.description: New canvas width in px: a multiple of 4, 8-256 (objects: 8-400).

height.description: New canvas height in px: a multiple of 4, 8-256 (objects: 8-400).

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__set_character_portrait
tools.description:
Attach a bust portrait to a character, or remove the portrait or one of its
talking expressions (no generation, free).

A portrait is the starting frame for talking animations — set one, then
create_vocal_animation generates the mouth positions from it. Overwrites any
existing portrait. Pass exactly one of image, from_job_id, remove_portrait or
remove_expression.

Examples:
- Straight from a portrait job:
  set_character_portrait("<character-uuid>", from_job_id="<portrait-job-uuid>")
- From your own artwork:
  set_character_portrait("<character-uuid>", image=<png_base64>)
- Delete the portrait:
  set_character_portrait("<character-uuid>", remove_portrait=True)
- Delete the angry expression, keep the rest:
  set_character_portrait("<character-uuid>", remove_expression="angry")

character_id.description: Character whose portrait (or expression) to set or remove.

image.description: Portrait as base64-encoded PNG. Square is ideal; a non-square image is centred on a transparent square canvas.

from_job_id.description: Instead of `image`: the job id of a completed create_portrait_character run. The sprite is copied straight across, so it never has to pass through your context.

remove_portrait.description: Delete the character's portrait instead of setting one. Expressions already made from it stay and keep working with create_talking_gif and get_lip_sync; a new expression needs a portrait again.

remove_expression.description: Delete this one expression (mood) from the character's mouth positions instead. The others stay, and the rows below it in the spritesheet move up; removing the last one removes the whole set. Make it again with create_vocal_animation.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__transfer_outfit
tools.description:
Reskin an existing animation with the outfit from a reference image (pro).

Every frame keeps its pose and motion; only the appearance changes to match
the reference — new armour on a walk cycle, a new colour scheme across an
attack, a weapon carried through the whole sequence.

transfer_outfit(frame_urls=[<f1>, <f2>, ...], reference_image_url=<outfit>)

The reference should be the SAME character in the new outfit. It does not
reliably turn one character into another.

Which edit tool:
- one image, or the same edit on separate images: edit_image
  (edit_image(reference_image_base64=...) copies an outfit onto ONE image)
- an animation's frames, changed by a text instruction: edit_animation
- an animation's frames, re-dressed from a reference image: transfer_outfit
  (this)

Needs 2+ frames. For a stored character's animation pass its frame URLs from
get_character.

Frame limit depends on output size (the reference takes one grid slot):
both sides 32-64px up to 15 frames, both 65-80px up to 8, larger side
81-256px up to 3. Frames over the limit: split across calls with the same
reference and seed.

For a console or palette look (1-bit, Game Boy, PICO-8, any palette from
Lospec) pass `palette` as its hex colours plus `palette_name`: every pixel of
every frame is one of them (the palette, not the reference, sets the colours).

Needs a tier 1 subscription or higher.
Cost: billed by the whole grid, not the frame count — 2 frames cost the same
as 15 at 64x64, so batch them. One ascending ladder by FRAME size, both sides
counting: 32-128 px: 10 | 129-170: 15 | 171-256: 25. So 96x96 and 128x128 are
both 10 while 160x160 is 15 and 200x200 is 25 — these are NOT edit_image's
bands (that tool stays 10 all the way to 256x256), because above 80px the
reference and the frames always share a 2x2 sheet here. Frames per call: 15
up to 64px, 8 up to 80, 3 above, the reference taking one cell.
