tools.name: mcp__pixellab__get_map
tools.description:
Show a map as an ASCII grid, one character per terrain cell.

With no crop you get the whole map downsampled to fit; pass x/y/width/height
for a 1:1 view of one area. Coordinates are terrain cells and can be
negative — the rulers show the real numbers, so read them off the view and
pass them straight to edit_map.

Maps built from tile groups (isometric, hex, oblique and similar tiles) show
their tile layers: for every cell the tile on top and the stack level it
sits on, plus each stacked column spelled out. Change those with
place_map_tiles.

export="godot" / "unity" / "pixellab" returns a download link for the map
as a game-engine project or the PixelLab ZIP instead of the view.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__get_object
tools.description:
Get object details. Branches by status:
- processing: progress + ETA
- review: candidate frame URLs + inline previews
- expanding / review-expansion: an 8-direction expansion
  (expand_object_to_8_directions) running, then waiting to be kept or discarded
- completed: rotation URLs, animations, download link
- failed: error + retry hint

Download: `/mcp/objects/{id}/download` is a ZIP holding
`rotations/<direction>.png` and
`animations/<name>/<direction>/frame_000.png` (frame_NNN, 3 digits, from
000) at the ZIP root — flatter than the character ZIP, and with no
metadata.json. A one-direction object with no animations comes back as a
bare PNG instead of a ZIP. `/mcp/objects/{id}/spritesheet` is a ZIP of one
sheet PNG + layout JSON: one row per animation-direction, uniform cells
sized to the largest frame (nothing resized), `pivot: "cell-center"`.
To get an animation's pixels INLINE, with no download and nothing charged:
`pixelart_workbench(argv=["inspect", "object:<id>:<direction>:<animation>"])`
returns its frames as one sheet image in the tool result. A one-direction
object still needs the direction, and it is the literal `unknown` —
`object:<id>:unknown:<group id>`. `join ref ref --as rows` lays several
animations out one per row (at most 1024 px a side).

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__get_room
tools.description:
A room's state. While it is being made: its stage and progress. When ready: the room
as painted (inline), its download link and its building kit's (a ZIP of the wall, door
and floor tiles it was built from); once its furniture is cut out
(cut_out_room_furniture), its movable pieces by name and the link that opens it in the
website's room editor (move, remove or bring in pieces; shadows follow).

Download: the room as painted is the `download:` PNG. Its cut-out pieces and its
furniture-free floor are in the `layers:` JSON this prints once the pieces are ready
(public, no auth) — you do not need the editor to export them. Keys: `w`/`h` the
room's pixel size; `room` the painting as you see it; `lit` and `unlit` the SAME room
with every piece removed (the empty floor, lit and unlit); `sprites[]` one entry per
piece with `name`, `x`,`y` (its top-left in those pixels), `foot` (the y of its
LOWEST OPAQUE row, where it stands on the floor — not `y` + the PNG's height,
which may end in transparent rows; sort pieces by it to draw them back to front),
`light`, `img` (a transparent PNG as a data URL), `unlit`, and `shadow` {`x`,`y`,`f`}
as its own PNG at its own position, or null where a piece casts none. An isometric room also has `over`: its low front curbs, which go on
top of the pieces. Every image is a `data:image/png;base64,` URL, so decode it rather
than fetching a second file.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__get_topdown_tileset
tools.description:

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__get_upload_url
tools.description:
Get a URL to upload a local image file to, without needing your API token.

Use it whenever you have an image on disk and a tool wants an image: send
the file with one curl, and pass the `upload:<id>` it returns to any

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__image_to_pixelart
tools.description:
Convert an image, render or photo into pixel art.

This is the general-purpose converter: give it any picture and get pixel art
back at the size you ask for. Use it when a user brings their own artwork,
a screenshot, or an AI render and wants it as a sprite.

Two dials decide how much licence the model takes:
- default (faithful=False, init_image_strength=0) — reinterprets the subject
  as pixel art. Cleanest sprites, least like the original.
- faithful=True with init_image_strength around 100-300 — reproduces the
  source. Use it when the user says "keep it exactly like this". Higher is
  NOT more faithful in a useful way: past ~300 the model stops transforming
  and returns the source image, which is not pixel art.

This is the one converter where YOU pick the output size. When the size does
not matter, image_to_pixelart_pro_flash (6 generations) and
image_to_pixelart_pro (20, tier 1+) redraw more cleanly and pick the size from
the picture.

Related tools: create_portrait_character converts a picture into a character
portrait specifically; unzoom_image is what you want if the input is ALREADY
pixel art that has merely been upscaled — running it through here would
redraw art that only needed downscaling.

Input max area 2048x2048, output max 512x512.

Cost: 1 generation. Generation time: ~20-60 seconds (async).
Poll with get_image(job_id).

image_base64.description: Base64 PNG/JPEG of the image to convert. Any artwork, render or photo. PREFER image_url — MCP clients routinely truncate large inline base64.

image_url.description: Alternative to image_base64: an https, data: or `upload:<id>` URL to the source image. PREFER THIS for anything but a tiny sprite. Give one, not both.

output_width.description: Width of the pixel art result. Defaults to a quarter of the source width. Keep the source's aspect ratio.

output_height.description: Height of the pixel art result. Defaults to a quarter of the source height.

project_id.description: Internal Game Builder project context; the finished image is linked after generation.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__image_to_pixelart_pro
tools.description:
Convert a picture, render or photo into pixel art with the Pro converter —
the strongest redraw of the three converters.

Which converter:
- image_to_pixelart (1 generation): you choose the exact output width and
  height; faithful mode keeps the source's look. Use it when the size matters.
- image_to_pixelart_pro_flash (6 generations): a clean redraw, output size
  picked from the picture. The default when the size does not matter.
- image_to_pixelart_pro (this, 20 generations, tier 1+): the same automatic
  size, the most careful redraw. Use it when pro_flash's result is not good
  enough.
None of them is for art that is already pixel art but upscaled — that only
needs unzoom_image.

The output size is decided by the conversion (the detected pixel scale) and
reported by get_image. For a console or palette look (1-bit, Game Boy, PICO-8,
any palette from Lospec) pass `palette` as its hex colours plus `palette_name`:
every pixel of the result is one of them. Transparent areas of the source
become a white background. Sources over 2048px on the longest side are scaled
down first.

Needs a tier 1 subscription or higher.
Cost: 20 generations at any source size. ~1-3 minutes (async). Poll
get_image(job_id).

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__inpaint_image
tools.description:
Regenerate one region of an image, keeping everything else pixel-identical.

This is the repair tool: fix a malformed hand, erase a stray pixel cluster,
swap just the cape, add an item to a specific spot. The area outside the
mask is frozen, so the rest of the sprite cannot drift.

Give the area as a rectangle (easiest — you only need coordinates):
  inpaint_image(image_base64=<png>, description="a clean open hand",
                mask_x=18, mask_y=30, mask_width=14, mask_height=14)
or supply your own mask (white = regenerate, black = keep):
  inpaint_image(image_base64=<png>, description="...", mask_image_base64=<png>)

Related: edit_image rewrites the WHOLE image from an instruction (no mask);
create_map_object generates a new object matching a background's style and
returns a transparent cutout, not your edited image.

Image must be 32x32-512x512; above 256px on a side needs a Tier 2 plan.
Cost: 10 generations for any SQUARE canvas up to 256x256 (so 64x64 and 88x88
are both 10), 15 up to 341x341, 25 above. The whole image sets the price, not
the mask. A NON-SQUARE canvas is measured against the nearest of ten aspect
ratios, so BOTH sides count and neither the longest side nor the area decides
it. The 10 ceiling then the 15 ceiling, by ratio: 1:1 256x256 then 341x341 |
5:4 288x232 then 384x309 | 4:3 300x224 then 400x298 | 3:2 316x212 then
421x282 | 16:9 344x192 then 458x256 | 21:9 396x168 then 528x224 (that last
one is past this tool's own 512px side limit, so it is unreachable); a portrait
canvas takes its own ratio's pair swapped (4:5, 3:4, 2:3, 9:16, and anything
taller than 9:16 snaps to 9:16). A canvas fitting inside a ceiling costs that
band and anything past the second one is 25, so 360x168 is 10 and 168x360 is
15, and 220x256 is 10 where 220x400 is 15 and 220x512 is 25.
Generation time: ~30-90 seconds (async).
Poll with get_image(job_id).

description.description: What should appear in the masked area (e.g. 'a clean four-finger hand holding a sword', 'plain grass, no object').

image_base64.description: Base64 PNG to repair. 32x32 to 512x512. Everything outside the mask is preserved exactly. PREFER image_url — MCP clients routinely truncate large inline base64, which corrupts the image.

image_url.description: Alternative to image_base64: an https, data: or `upload:<id>` URL to the PNG to repair. PREFER THIS for anything but a tiny sprite — inline base64 is often cut off mid-string by MCP clients. Give one, not both.

mask_x.description: Left edge of the rectangular area to regenerate.

mask_y.description: Top edge of the rectangular area to regenerate.

mask_width.description: Width of the area to regenerate.

mask_height.description: Height of the area to regenerate.

mask_image_url.description: Alternative to mask_image_base64: an https, data: or `upload:<id>` URL to the mask PNG. Give one, not both.

crop_to_mask.description: Confine generated content to the mask boundary for clean edges.

no_background.description: Background handling. Default (unset) follows the input: a sprite with transparency stays transparent, an opaque image stays opaque. Pass False to flatten a transparent input onto white.

project_id.description: Internal Game Builder project context; the finished image is linked after generation.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__inpaint_image_pro_flash
tools.description:
Replace white-mask pixels with Pro Flash, preserving unmasked RGBA bytes exactly.

Source: image_url, image_base64, or owned source_image_id. Mask: a rectangle
(all four mask_x/y/width/height), OR a same-size mask PNG via base64/URL.
Mask RGB must be pure white=generate or black=keep; mask alpha is ignored.
Empty masks are rejected. crop_to_mask is always true. Changes-only output
is transparent outside the mask; Modify current layer returns a composite.
Optional context_image requires bounding_box locating the source and is at
most three times its native dimensions. No images or masks are rescaled.
Query get_pro_flash_capabilities for shapes; poll the job with get_image.

Cost: by the SOURCE canvas's longest side, not the mask — 5 generations up to
96px, 6 from 100 to 208, 9 from 212 to 256, for one image. So a 64x64 repair
is 5 and 128x64 is 6, against inpaint_image's 10 for either. Shrinking the
mask does not lower it. get_pro_flash_capabilities(operation="inpaint",
width=, height=) prices an exact size for free.

mask_image_base64.description: Mask PNG, exactly the source size. EVERY pixel's RGB must be pure white (generate) or pure black (keep): a grey or coloured pixel is refused, so remove any antialiasing, and a mask with no white at all is refused too. The mask's own alpha is ignored. Unlike inpaint_image, which does not check this, Pro Flash enforces it. Or give the four mask_x/y/width/height instead.

mask_image_url.description: Same mask as mask_image_base64, from an https, data: or `upload:<id>` URL.

context_image.description: The surrounding scene to match, not a style reference. Pass it WITH bounding_box or not at all. At most 3x the source canvas in each dimension and never rescaled. Exactly ONE of its three sources.

usage_description.description: How this reference should guide appearance.

bounding_box.description: Where the source canvas sits inside context_image: width/height must equal the source size, and the box must lie entirely within the context image.

no_background.description: Background removal on the GENERATED pixels. Left out it follows the source: on if the source has any non-opaque pixel, off if it is fully opaque. Removal runs before the frozen pixels are copied back, so masked pixels CAN come back transparent (how a bigger hairstyle keeps gaps around it) and pixels outside the mask are untouched either way. Off, the render is drawn on a background, so the masked area comes back opaque.

output_method.description: What comes back, always at the source's own size. `Modify current layer` (default) is the whole sprite with the mask area replaced. `Modify current layer, only changes` and `New layer with changes` are that same canvas holding ONLY the masked pixels, fully transparent everywhere else - a layer to drop over your own art. Every pixel outside the mask is copied from your source byte for byte, and that copy is the LAST step, after background removal and palette work, so nothing outside the mask can shift.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__inpaint_map
tools.description:
Regenerate one rectangular area of a map with AI — a ramp, a broken wall, a
path through a forest, a seam between two terrains — the way Map Workshop's
inpainting does. Give the area in the same cells get_map and edit_map use.

Choosing the area: put what you want near its centre and make it a bit
larger than that, with a cell or two of the map you keep on every side. The
model blends the new pixels into what it sees at the area's edges; something
that runs into an edge (a stream, a wall) can end in a visible step where the
area stops.

The new pixels go into the map's inpainted layer, which sits over the
terrain and under objects, exactly where Map Workshop puts its own
inpainting; the terrain cells underneath are unchanged.

Cost: like inpaint_image_pro_flash, by the area's longest side in pixels — 5
generations up to 96px, 6 up to 208px, 9 up to 256px. Not available on
sidescroller maps or maps with tile layers (the area could not be drawn here
as Map Workshop shows it).

Non-blocking: returns a job_id. Poll inpaint_map(map_id=..., job_id=...);
when the job completes the result is written into the map (also
automatically) and the poll shows the area.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__make_music_loop
tools.description:
Make one of your songs into game music that loops seamlessly.

The song is made again so that the part between its intro and its ending
repeats without a seam: two new takes, each with loop points. Play the take to
loop_end, then jump back to loop_start (get_music shows both, in seconds). The
intro plays once, the ending never. Instrumental songs only, for now.

Cost: 4 generations, or $0.033 in credits; charged once the takes are made.
Needs a tier 2 subscription or higher.

Generation time: ~1.5-2.5 minutes (async). Poll with get_music or wait_for_jobs.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__pixelart_workbench
tools.description:
Run one pixel-art command on a drawing or image you already made. This is
the engine's own command line: it checks work, explains it and improves it.

Commands: check and explain (read-only):
- lint <id> [--rules outline_gap,orphan_pixel,...] — pixel-art defects, each
  naming the node and command that drew them
- inspect <id> --region x0,y0,x1,y1 --scale 10 — a zoomed crop with its
  exact colours, to LOOK at: the id it returns still holds the whole
  picture, so passing it on sends the full canvas and not the region.
  `split ... --count` below is what actually cuts a piece out
- measure <id> --at x,y — what is at a pixel and who drew it
- explain <id> — resolved geometry, per-command footprints, before rendering
- motion / storyboard / silhouette / reveal / clusters / parts <id> — reports
- score <id> — a 0-100 pixel-art discipline score with a breakdown
- compare <id> <id> — two results side by side
Improve (returns a NEW drawing id):
- shade <id> --band 2 --light=-1,-1 — banded shading along a colour ramp
- selout <id> — selective outlining; reoutline / clean-lines / aa / mirror
- cluster <id> --at x,y --action recolor --color <name> — one guarded cluster
- repair <id> — deterministic cleanup of drift, strays, fringe and noise
Sheets and frames (returns a NEW image id):
- split <image> --grid 3x3 [--count n] — a sprite sheet, strip or grid as an
  animation, one frame per cell (columns x rows). --count keeps the first n
  cells and drops the rest, so `split <image> --grid 2x1 --count 1` is the
  free exact crop of the left half, `--grid 1x2 --count 1` the top half, and
  a one-cell result downloads as image.png (a multi-frame one has no
  image.png, only frames.png — which is why a plain 2x1 split cannot be
  handed on as a single picture). Cells must divide the canvas evenly; the
  error names the counts that fit. Without --count, trailing cells that are
  one flat colour are dropped
- join <image> <image> ... [--as sheet|rows|animation] [--columns n] — pictures
  or animations as one sprite sheet, one per row, or one animation
- scale <image> --by 4 — the same picture or animation bigger, each pixel a
  4x4 block (a sticker, a print); nothing is redrawn
A result comes back as an image in the reply AND as a no-auth URL the reply
prints, `/mcp/pixel-tools/<id>/image.png` (`frames.png` for the frames of a
multi-frame one) — so a sheet you joined is both readable inline and
downloadable. Sheets hold at most 1024 px a side; `join` refuses a larger
one rather than shrinking the art, and says how many frames do fit.
Craft operations need colour ramps: run `extract-palette <id>` first, then
pass `--ramps skin=dark,mid,light`.
Authoring: `edit <id> --changes '[...]'` applies exact pixel operations and
`draw <id> --recipe '{...}'` builds or revises a layered scene; both take JSON
whose fields are NOT listed here. Colours in that JSON are always `#RRGGBB`
or `#RRGGBBAA` with alpha `00` or `ff` — `rgb()` and bare hex are refused,
and nothing strips the `#`, since argv is a JSON list rather than a shell
line. Every `edit` change carries `operation`, `layer`, `frames` (ONE-based)
and `reason`; coordinates are zero-based and a `region` is `[x0,y0,x1,y1]`
inclusive. Then its own fields: `patch_pixels` takes `pixels`, a list of
`[x,y,expected,replacement]` (1-10000, each assigned only where the pixel
already holds `expected`, so a mismatch fails the pass); `copy_region` takes
`source_layer`, `source_frame`, `region`, `at` `[x,y]`; `map_colors` takes
`region` and `colors` `{"#from":"#to"}` (alpha must match); `flood_fill`
`seed`/`expected`/`color`; `brush` `points` plus `color`; `outline` `mode`
(outside|inside|recolor|erase). The full contracts and any command's flags
are one free call away: `describe edits | paint | outline | draw | animation
| motion | scenes | review`, `<command> -h`, `describe cli`.
Free for subscribers.

`seed`/`expected`/`color`; `brush` `points` plus `color`; `outline` `mode`
(outside|inside|recolor|erase). The full contracts and any command's flags
are one free call away: `describe edits | paint | outline | draw | animation
| motion | scenes | review`, `<command> -h`, `describe cli`.
Free for subscribers.

argv.description: One command line, e.g. 'lint <drawing_id> --rules outline_gap' or ['edit', '<id>', '--changes', '[...]']. Omit it for the playbook. A subject is an id or an image reference — never a file path; the server writes the output and returns a new id. A reference is `character:<id>:<direction>` for a rotation, `character:<id>:<direction>:<animation>` for every frame of that animation (the display name, type or [group: ...] id get_character prints), the same two forms for `object:<id>` (a one-direction object's direction is the literal `unknown`), `gallery:<id>`, `job:<id>`, `upload:<id>`, a data URL, an https link or base64. That is how a stored animation's pixels come back inline without downloading anything. Start with 'describe cli' for the full command list.

mode.description: low (default): act directly, fewest tokens — one decisive image per result. high: think openly — fuller evidence and a review checklist; write your plan and observations in `notes`. Use the mode the user asked for.

notes.description: What you observed and what this step should achieve, in a few sentences (high mode: always; low: optional). On the first call, include the user's request. Stored with the step to improve these tools.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__place_map_object
tools.description:
Place objects or characters on a map, at a terrain cell or an exact pixel.

Objects are how a map gets trees, houses, rocks and NPCs — terrain painting
(edit_map) only covers ground. A tileset tiles a SURFACE, so anything with a
silhouette has to be an object.

Position: x/y stands the sprite on that cell (the coordinates get_map
shows). world_x/world_y puts it at an exact world pixel instead, as Map
Workshop's free drag does — use it to match positions from a game scene or
an isometric layout that does not fall on the cell grid.

For many objects pass `placements`: one call, one save.

Returns a picture of the result by default, because a placement that is one
cell off, or far bigger than you expected, is invisible in text.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__place_map_tiles
tools.description:
Place, stack and erase tiles on a map's tile layers — the map editor's tile
painting, with its Stack layer control.

A map made from tile groups (isometric, hex, oblique, square tiles) keeps
each group as a tile layer; get_map lists them and shows, per cell, the
tile on top and its stack level. A cell holds a column of tiles: level 0
is the ground, and each level above sits one tile height higher, so a
`stack` of 3 builds a pillar and "on_top" builds on whatever is there.

Placing on a cell's level replaces the tile already there. As in the
editor, a tile placed on one ground layer clears that same cell and level
on any other ground layer drawn on the same grid.

Tiles go down exactly as given: for connected sets, pick the tile drawn
for that spot's neighbours (get_tiles_pro lists each tile's mask).

A building kit is several layers: floor, interior walls, outer walls, roof
(when the kit has roof pieces) and pieces (pillars, doorways, stairs). Lay
floor tiles and the outer walls follow the floor's outline. Interior walls
and roofs take no tile: each cell's piece follows its neighbours. A doorway
is cut into the wall at that cell, and stairs lay both halves. get_map lists
what each kit layer takes.

Returns what changed and a view of the area: the top tile and the top
level of every cell, and each stacked column level by level.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__reduce_colors
tools.description:
Quantize images onto a smaller, shared palette.

Pixel art reads as pixel art partly because of its restricted palette. AI
output and converted artwork often carry hundreds of near-identical colors;
this snaps them onto a tight palette, optionally with ordered dithering.

Passing several frames in one call is the point: they are quantized TOGETHER,
so an animation or a character's eight directions come back sharing ONE
palette instead of drifting apart frame by frame. Quantizing them one at a
time is the mistake this tool exists to prevent.

Three ways to choose the palette:
- omit num_colors and the palette image — the size is auto-detected
- num_colors — quantize to exactly this many colors
- palette_image — reuse the colors of an existing image (the game's palette)

The result carries a `palette` strip you can feed back as palette_image_base64
to lock later frames onto the same colors.

Total size limit across all frames is 512x512 worth of pixels (sixteen 64x64
frames, or four 128x128).

Cost: 0.1 generations. Runs locally in about a second — poll once with
get_image(job_id).

images_base64.description: Base64 PNG(s) to quantize — pass a one-element list for a single image. All frames must be the same size. PREFER image_urls; MCP clients routinely truncate large inline base64.

palette_image_base64.description: Base64 PNG whose colors become the palette (max 256 colors) — use it to force frames onto an existing game palette. Cannot be combined with num_colors.

palette_image_url.description: Alternative to palette_image_base64: an https, data: or `upload:<id>` URL to the palette image. Give one, not both.

dithering.description: Ordered dithering matrix size. Larger matrices give smoother gradients at the cost of a busier look.

dithering_strength.description: How strongly to dither. Ignored when dithering is 'none'.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__remove_background
tools.description:
Remove the background from an image you already have, leaving the subject on
transparency. Same size in and out.

The generators' no_background=True only applies while they draw. Use this for
an image that already exists: one from the gallery or another tool that came
back on a backdrop, an uploaded sprite sheet frame, a screenshot, a picture a
user brought.

Max 400x400 in area (e.g. 400x400, 200x800). One image per call.

Cost: 1 generation. Usually ~10-30 seconds (async). Poll get_image(job_id).

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__remove_from_project
tools.description:
Stop a game project from using a character, object, tileset, map, room, UI
asset, song or sound effect, or take an asset out of a folder (or a tile group
or isometric tile out of the game it is filed under).

This unlinks the art from the project. It does NOT delete the art: the
asset stays in your library and can be added back at any time, and any
other project using it is untouched. Use delete_character / delete_object /
delete_topdown_tileset / delete_map / delete_room to actually destroy something.

Until now add_to_project had no inverse, so a project could accumulate art
it no longer used — and a map that fails to export blocks every deploy of
that project, with no way back out.

The kind is worked out from the id; you do not have to say which it is.
Calling twice is harmless.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__save_to_asset
tools.description:
Save pixel art into one of your characters, objects, Creator gallery
images or tilesets, replacing a rotation, one direction of an animation, a
gallery image or a tileset's tiles — or add it to the gallery as a new image
(free, no generation).

Use it to keep a fix made with pixelart_workbench or another image tool: the
character and object creators, the Creator gallery, the map editor, downloads
and game projects then show the new pixels. The image must match what it replaces —
the same canvas size and the same number of frames; a different size can go
to the gallery as a new image. Save each direction with its own call. The
replaced frames are kept: the reply gives the save_to_asset call that puts
them back.

Examples:
- save_to_asset(image="<workbench id>", target="character:<id>:south")
- save_to_asset(image="<workbench id>", target="character:<id>:east:<group id>")
- save_to_asset(image="<workbench id>", target="object:<id>")
- save_to_asset(image="<workbench id>", target="gallery:<id>")
- save_to_asset(image="<workbench id>", target="gallery:new",
  description="knight holding a sword, idle")
- save_to_asset(image="<edited sheet>", target="tileset:<id>")

images or tilesets, replacing a rotation, one direction of an animation, a
gallery image or a tileset's tiles — or add it to the gallery as a new image
(free, no generation).

Use it to keep a fix made with pixelart_workbench or another image tool: the
character and object creators, the Creator gallery, the map editor, downloads
and game projects then show the new pixels. The image must match what it replaces —
the same canvas size and the same number of frames; a different size can go
to the gallery as a new image. Save each direction with its own call. The
replaced frames are kept: the reply gives the save_to_asset call that puts
them back.

Examples:
- save_to_asset(image="<workbench id>", target="character:<id>:south")
- save_to_asset(image="<workbench id>", target="character:<id>:east:<group id>")
- save_to_asset(image="<workbench id>", target="object:<id>")

- save_to_asset(image="<workbench id>", target="gallery:new",
  description="knight holding a sword, idle")

image.description: What to save: a pixelart_workbench result id (`<id>`, or `<id>:<view>` for a drawing), `job:<id>` / `job:<id>:<index>` (an image tool result), `upload:<id>` (an image POSTed to /v2/uploads), an https or data URL of a PNG or GIF, or base64. A PNG is one frame, even a strip: an animation's frames go as a GIF (one duration for all), a multi-image `job:<id>` or a multi-frame pixelart_workbench result.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__select_object_frames
tools.description:
Promote selected frames of a review object to individual completed objects.

See get_object on a review-status object to view candidates inline.
Each selected index becomes its own 1-direction object. Once no frames
remain in the review object it is deleted automatically. If a call times

review-expansion), call it with no indices to keep the expansion: the same
object becomes 8-direction, its canvas grows to the review's size and its

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__set_canvas_size
tools.description:
Change a character's or object's canvas size by adding or removing transparent margin. Free.

Every rotation is re-centred on the new canvas about its pivot. The art is
never scaled or cropped: a size smaller than the art itself is refused with
the art's bounds. Animations keep the canvas they were made on; an object's
map placements follow it. Use it to give a sprite room before animating
(a sword swing, a jump) or to trim empty margin.

tools.description:

talking expressions (no generation, free).

A portrait is the starting frame for talking animations — set one, then
create_vocal_animation generates the mouth positions from it. Overwrites any
existing portrait. Pass exactly one of image, from_job_id, remove_portrait or

Examples:
- Straight from a portrait job:

- From your own artwork:

- Delete the portrait:
  set_character_portrait("<character-uuid>", remove_portrait=True)
- Delete the angry expression, keep the rest:

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__transfer_outfit
tools.description:
Reskin an existing animation with the outfit from a reference image (pro).

Every frame keeps its pose and motion; only the appearance changes to match
the reference — new armour on a walk cycle, a new colour scheme across an
attack, a weapon carried through the whole sequence.

transfer_outfit(frame_urls=[<f1>, <f2>, ...], reference_image_url=<outfit>)

The reference should be the SAME character in the new outfit. It does not
reliably turn one character into another.

Which edit tool:
- one image, or the same edit on separate images: edit_image
  (edit_image(reference_image_base64=...) copies an outfit onto ONE image)
- an animation's frames, changed by a text instruction: edit_animation
- an animation's frames, re-dressed from a reference image: transfer_outfit
  (this)

Needs 2+ frames. For a stored character's animation pass its frame URLs from
get_character.

Frame limit depends on output size (the reference takes one grid slot):
both sides 32-64px up to 15 frames, both 65-80px up to 8, larger side
81-256px up to 3. Frames over the limit: split across calls with the same
reference and seed.

For a console or palette look (1-bit, Game Boy, PICO-8, any palette from
Lospec) pass `palette` as its hex colours plus `palette_name`: every pixel of
every frame is one of them (the palette, not the reference, sets the colours).

Needs a tier 1 subscription or higher.
Cost: billed by the whole grid, not the frame count — 2 frames cost the same
as 15 at 64x64, so batch them. One ascending ladder by FRAME size, both sides
counting: 32-128 px: 10 | 129-170: 15 | 171-256: 25. So 96x96 and 128x128 are
both 10 while 160x160 is 15 and 200x200 is 25 — these are NOT edit_image's
bands (that tool stays 10 all the way to 256x256), because above 80px the
reference and the frames always share a 2x2 sheet here. Frames per call: 15
up to 64px, 8 up to 80, 3 above, the reference taking one cell.
Generation time: ~1-2 minutes (async).
Poll with get_image(job_id); frames come back in input order.

frames_base64.description: Base64 PNG animation frames to reskin, in order (2 or more). Max 256x256 each. PREFER frame_urls — MCP clients routinely truncate large inline base64.

frame_urls.description: Alternative to frames_base64: https, data: or `upload:<id>` (POST /v2/uploads with this same bearer token) URLs to the frame PNGs, in order. PREFER THIS for anything but tiny sprites. Give urls OR base64, not both.

reference_image_base64.description: Base64 PNG of the SAME character wearing the new outfit (e.g. a re-dressed or recoloured sprite of it). A different character as reference is unreliable — it can freeze the motion or barely change anything. Max 256x256.

reference_image_url.description: Alternative to reference_image_base64: an https, data: or `upload:<id>` URL to the reference PNG. PREFER THIS for anything but a tiny sprite. Give one, not both.

width.description: Output frame width. Defaults to the widest frame. Frames and reference smaller than this are padded with transparency, centred — never scaled.

height.description: Output frame height. Defaults to the tallest frame.

no_background.description: Background handling. Default (unset) follows the frames: if any frame has transparency the results are transparent, otherwise opaque. Pass False to flatten a transparent input onto white.

project_id.description: Internal Game Builder project context; the finished frames are linked after generation.

palette.description: Target palette, 2 to 256 hex colours as a JSON array, e.g. ["#081820", "#346856", "#88c070", "#e0f8d0"] for Game Boy or ["#000000", "#ffffff"] for 1-bit. Every pixel the tool draws is one of them; pixels you supplied (a direction you drew) stay as they are.

palette_name.description: Optional name of the palette (e.g. 'Game Boy', 'PICO-8'); naming it helps the look. It only LABELS the colours you pass in palette rather than looking any up, so it cannot be sent on its own.

max_colors.description: At most this many colours (2-64). With a palette, they are picked from it. On the three tools that have a standard mode — create_character, create_topdown_tileset, animate_object — ANY palette setting needs mode='pro': standard refuses palette and max_colors, alone or together. Every other tool taking them has no standard mode and accepts them always.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__unzoom_image
tools.description:
Downscale upscaled pixel art back onto its true pixel grid.

Pixel art found online is almost always scaled up — a 32x32 sprite saved at
512x512, where every art pixel is a 16x16 block. Every tool that takes a
reference or style image works far better on the real 32x32 sprite, and this
recovers it: the pixel grid is detected and the image is downsampled onto it.

Run this FIRST whenever a user supplies pixel art from outside PixelLab and
you are about to pass it to create_image_pixflux(init_image), a style image,
edit_image, or create_character. If the art was never upscaled it is already
at native size and this is unnecessary.

Do not confuse it with image_to_pixelart: that CONVERTS a non-pixel-art
picture, redrawing it. This one only downscales art that is already pixel art.
It always returns some grid: a result with nearly as many colours as pixels
means the input was not upscaled pixel art.

Input must be at least 256x256 (grid detection needs the pixels) and at most
2048x2048 in area.

The result is OPAQUE: transparency is composited onto white. If the user
needs a cut-out sprite, tell them.

Cost: 0.1 generations. Takes a few seconds at most — poll get_image(job_id).

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__update_ui_asset
tools.description:
Edit a UI asset, free (nothing is generated). One change per call:

- split=True: cut a template into elements, each its own UI asset (PNG) to place,
  9-slice, give hover/pressed states (create_ui_states) and download.
  get_ui_asset(template id) shows where it cuts first. To split differently,
  delete its elements first. Editing or deleting an element re-composes the
  template's image from its elements.
- nine_slice / clear_nine_slice: the border insets that stay crisp when a panel,
  button or bar is stretched to another size in a game. Stored with the asset:
  get_ui_asset, its ZIP's metadata.json and the /chat game's assets/ui/index.json
  carry it.

To rename a UI asset, use rename_asset.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__vfx_workbench
tools.description:
Make an animated pixel-art effect (spell, hit, explosion, aura, projectile,
weather...) yourself, around the user's sprite or on its own: drop in tuned
parts, write layers, look at every render, then export. Export saves it to the
user's My effects on pixellab.ai (re-editable there with sliders) and returns a
GIF and a spritesheet PNG + JSON; --game-pack adds a ZIP of every piece for a game
engine (--part <id> just one). Free for subscribers.

Commands:
- start [--sprite <image>] [--fps N] [--projectile <image>]
  [--preset <name> | --effect <effect id>] -> step id
- <step id> <tool> '<JSON>' -> add_part, set_part, remove_part, throw, render,
  get_preset, get_part, list_parts; a change returns a new step id
- <step id> export [--name N] [--replace <effect id>] [--game-pack | --part <id>]
- effects [--limit N] [--after <effect id>] -> the user's My effects (ids)
- delete <effect id> -> removes it from My effects for good
- describe start | parts | recipe | craft | cookbook | edits | presets | tools
Limits, which are this tool's own and NOT the website VFX Creator's: the
effect canvas is 16-1024 px a side in whole pixels (no multiple-of-4 rule
here), fps is 1-60 and defaults to 12, `loop` is a true/false field on the
recipe (default false; whole-number part cycle counts are what make a looping
one seamless), and frames go up to 120 under a pixel
budget of frames x width x height <= 32 x 1024 x 1024 — so 120 frames up to a
512 px canvas, 81 at 640, 56 at 768 and 32 at 1024. A `--sprite` is the
stricter one: at most 32 frames, each at most 512x512.
Sprites and exports are pixelart_workbench ids, so the two work together.
Start with describe start.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__view_map
tools.description:
Render the map to an image and return it, terrain and objects together.

Use this to judge how a map LOOKS — get_map's ASCII shows you where terrain
is, never what it looks like. Crop with x/y/width/height (the same cell
coordinates get_map and edit_map use) to inspect an area closely.

This renders from the terrain grid, so it always shows the map's CURRENT
state, including edits a human has not opened Map Workshop to see.
Sidescroller maps are not drawn: their side-view rules are not reproduced
here, so you get a note instead of a wrong picture.

tools.name: mcp__pixellab__wait_for_jobs
tools.description:
Wait for your running generations instead of sleeping and polling.

Returns as soon as min_finished (default 1) of your pending/processing jobs
finish, immediately when none are running, or at the timeout. Free. Then call
the matching get_* tool for the result; call wait_for_jobs again for the jobs
still running. It watches every job on the account, so it also lists ones the
user started on the website or with another client.

# Directional robot consumer observation

This bounded renderer loads the existing `src/robot.ts` controller, calls
`spriteFor` for south/east/north/west, and paints the actual destination PNGs at
1x and 3x nearest sampling on `#172336`. These scales and background are observation
conditions. They do not add an owner-approved palette or presentation requirement.
The original planning example stays unchanged; a production evaluation must supply
its own explicit assignment before generating the missing directions.

Run with Node supporting `node:module.stripTypeScriptTypes` and a locally installed
Chrome or Edge. No browser configuration or profile is shared with the user.
The checker uses the existing Python/Pillow environment.

```powershell
node examples/delegation/renderer/capture.mjs --project C:/ABS/CONSUMER --out C:/ABS/CONSUMER/work/robot-capture-01
.venv/Scripts/python.exe examples/delegation/renderer/check.py --project C:/ABS/CONSUMER --capture C:/ABS/CONSUMER/work/robot-capture-01 --out C:/ABS/CONSUMER/work/robot-check-01.json
```

An explicit `--browser C:/ABS/chrome.exe` may be supplied to capture. The output
directory and checker output must be new. Failures preserve their receipts; use a
new path after correction. For interactive inspection, run
`node examples/delegation/renderer/server.mjs --project C:/ABS/CONSUMER` and open
the printed loopback URL, then stop that server when finished.

Required inputs are `src/robot.ts`, `assets/robot-base.png`, and
`assets/robot/{south,east,north,west}.png`. The south file must preserve the exact
base bytes. Each directional output must be a visible transparent 32x32 RGBA PNG.
The actual controller export and `spriteFor` must map every direction to its
matching filename. Missing files, mapping changes, nontransparent images, wrong
dimensions, changed inputs, altered capture files, and mismatched screenshot
pixels fail the mechanical check.

`capture.json` retains observed mappings, source/output hashes, browser identity,
scaled canvas images and their screenshot positions. `inputs.json` binds the
pre-capture inputs and renderer sources; `execution.json` records completion and
owned browser/server/profile cleanup. The checker compares decoded source pixels,
alpha compositing, nearest scaling and screenshot crops independently with Pillow.

The report does **not** decide whether a direction looks correct, whether all views
preserve the robot's identity/volume, or whether the artwork is suitable. Inspect
the source and delivered images plus `destination.png`, then record the visual
review separately. Copying one sprite to every direction can pass the mechanical
checks and still fail that review. The synthetic test fixture does exactly that
to test rendering without claiming new art or directional acceptance.

This supports the existing example controller. It is not a new generic
`consumer-execute` profile or qualification of a separate game engine.

134

137	  "status": "partial",
138	  "caller": {
139	    "summary": "Candidate bytes are retained; required destination inspection remains unperformed.",
140	    "integration": {

142	      "summary": "No destination observation has been made for this assignment."
143	    },
144	    "issues": [
145	      {

   An ambiguous condition that could reject a valid alternative needs clearer wording;
   do not approve it by silently giving it a more permissive interpretation. Verify the
   correction in the returned artifact before marking the contract consistent.

For example, a requirement for a readable silhouette does not itself require an
outlined silhouette. Comparing two outline colours leaves the added outline rule
untested; a readable outline-free construction tests it. The specialist may still
recommend an outline for this sample and explain its artistic value. The comparison
preserves that expertise while accurately describing who chose it and what it binds.

Cover every rejection rule; group only genuinely identical ones. Retain the source
quote/bounds, literal delta, tested alternative and disposition together. A general
"the brief permits flexibility" statement or a prompt-choice label elsewhere cannot
cancel a restriction still present in an owner-authority acceptance condition.

Check the **review route** as well as the wording. A local mechanical check can
establish measured dimensions, frame counts or alpha values. It cannot decide which
shape is intentional foreground, whether a matte is unwanted, whether a silhouette
reads as the requested symbol, or whether an accent serves its role. For a mixed
criterion, either split the measurement and required visual judgment or set its mode
to `visual` (normally domain `visual` too). The runtime requires saved native/enlarged
candidate views for visual-mode or visual/continuity-domain reviews; labelling such a
condition `mechanical`/`local` bypasses that evidence requirement. A planning-only
correction must still specify the route its future acceptance will actually need.
Do not call a corrected contract operable merely because its source locators resolve.

When reviewing a specialist's response to a discrepancy, re-open the literal check.
An added attribution or a claim that a conventional construction excludes no valid
alternatives does not remove an unchanged mandatory recipe. Retain the source's
qualitative outcome as required and place the expert construction in a scoped proposal;
judge actual recognizability without declaring one geometric recipe universal.

Resolve every evidence-report diagnostic before calling a locator verified. For a
text citation, open the actual source, use its file-local inclusive bounds and save
those bounds in the corrected packet; a nearby matching sentence does not repair a
wrong range. An unresolved named or visual reference needs actual inspection and a
recorded finding. A source hash alone never verifies the cited location or its meaning.

The [delegation boundary](delegation.md#caller--specialist) distinguishes unchanged
historical evidence from the editable corrected proposal. A caller must not freeze
prior criterion text or authority in the new proposal; reassess those interpretations
against the source. Use the profile's visual-role distinctions when translating colour,
subject construction and transparency intent, rather than adding a construction rule.

If a contract defect is found after delivery, preserve the original request, plan,
verdicts and candidate. Save a corrected proposal and independent comparison as a new
artifact, explicitly distinguishing it from the historical contract used for delivery.
Do not create another provider job merely to correct documentation, transplant old
verdicts to new criteria, or silently rewrite durable completed work. Carry both the
historical identity and the correction's adoption scope in the exact handoff details.

Keep process requirements, output requirements and diagnostic proxies distinct. A required production route is checked through actual calls and downloaded-byte provenance; a property of the resulting image is evidence only when it establishes that claim. Do not silently turn a process restriction into an extra output-difference test, or a diagnostic into a rejection rule. Independent review uses the original source, not another agent's assertion that the rule is sourced.

Save a concise `caller-review.json` (or equivalent named fields) with reviewer role, reviewed packet hash, `consistent` / `changes_requested` / `needs_input`, per-criterion comparisons and other findings tied to request locations and source evidence, and the next action. `consistent` means the planned contract matches this assignment; it is not provider execution or asset acceptance.

If changes are needed, send the specialist the precise discrepancy and relevant source; preserve the original artifacts, revise only the affected contract, and inspect the returned new packet. Reuse the existing specialist when the host supports it. Resolve supplied facts yourself; ask the user only a consequential decision genuinely missing from the available context. No token, secret header or credential belongs in either file.

If no independent caller/reviewer exists, retain the specialist's own review as self-review, proceed within existing authorization, and report the independent comparison as unperformed. Do not invent another agent or stop ordinary direct work solely to satisfy this procedure.

## Carry the comparison through production

Return `request_review` in the normal result, containing the packet and caller-review paths/hashes and unresolved findings. After preparing the durable provider job, verify its actual request still matches the reviewed arguments. A changed requirement, criterion or request needs a new comparison; polling progress and unrelated queue changes do not.

The final caller opens the delivered assets, checks the actual request and output against this contract, and records its own observations. Keep contract consistency, provider outcome, visual quality and destination acceptance separate. For a rejected candidate, retain the failure and the revised request/criteria; changing a checker merely to pass the candidate is a contract change, not an asset correction.

When an artistic explanation asserts a measurement, compare that assertion with
its actual data and coordinate convention. Reproducing a bounding box does not
verify a stated axis angle or arm-length ratio; approximate visual descriptions
should remain approximate. Correct an inconsistent explanation in a new observation
without converting its sample geometry into an additional rejection condition.
Reassess the original claim using its stated inputs. For quoted endpoints, retain
the coordinate convention and calculate their deltas, lengths and angles before
confirming an axis or ratio. Counts of occupied pixels, a bounding box and a newly
estimated centreline measure different things; they cannot confirm the original
endpoint claim. Save the old claim, calculation and corrected interpretation together
so the caller can reproduce the comparison without inheriting the earlier assertion.

## Start a successor comparison with the concise view

For two retained connected plans, call `pixl_request_review` with `view:"changes"`,
`plan` and explicit `against_plan`; CLI: `request-review STATE --plan NEW --against-plan OLD --view changes --root ROOT`.
Save with `result_path` / `--result-path`. Use the change counts, retained choices,
source drift and review attention to choose what to inspect. Then follow both
full-report retrievals and compare the exact literal criteria. The compact view
does not declare semantic equivalence, direct succession, consistency or approval.
All old/new IDs/hashes remain indexed; renamed clauses require explicit mapping.

Focused `pixl_context(view:"authoring")` expands explicitly linked choices and
their authority dependencies. Inspect `choice_scope.other_intake` when an unlinked
caller choice may apply; its retrieval links preserve access to the full record.
Do not promote observed/proposed values to confirmed requirements or infer that
an omitted full value is irrelevant. Keep the independent caller's interpretation
separate from the tool's deterministic structural comparison.

# Compact caller result

`plar handoff DETAILS_JSON --view caller` / `pixl_plar_handoff` with
`view: "caller"` saves the existing immutable version-1 handoff, then returns a
bounded presentation of that same captured selection. The default `view: "receipt"`
and saved bytes for identical inputs are unchanged. There is no new ledger, UDL
record, provider action or acceptance event.

## Agent-authored compact fields

`details.status` retains its existing assignment meaning: `delivered`, `partial`,
`needs_input` or `blocked`. It does not follow automatically from production state.
An optional `details.caller` object supplies the following closed fields:

| Field | Content |
| --- | --- |
| `summary` | Nonempty text, at most 600 characters |
| `artifacts` | At most 12 actual project file references |
| `reports` | At most 12 references to separately retained detailed reports |
| `issues` | At most 12 objects with `category`, `summary` and optional `recovery` |
| `integration` | An agent observation with `status`, `summary` and optional `evidence` file references |

All fields are optional. Omission means not reported, not a pass or an unavailable
check. An absent caller block is returned as `caller.present: false`; arbitrary
legacy details are never heuristically summarized. Existing receipt mode does not
reinterpret a legacy field called `caller`.

File references contain exactly `path`, `sha256` and `role`. Paths are nonempty
forward-slash project-relative paths, at most 512 characters. SHA-256 is 64 lowercase
hexadecimal digits; role is nonempty text of at most 96 characters. The operation
confines and hashes every declared artifact, report and integration-evidence file
before publishing. It does not copy those files or guarantee that they remain
unchanged after that observation. Roles and judgments are supplied by the agent.

Issue categories are `invalid_authoring`, `stale_local_state`, `missing_capability`,
`uncertain_remote_result`, `unavailable_observation` and `unfinished_work`.
Summary and recovery text each have the same 600-character bound. The category is
an agent's classification, not an automatic diagnosis or authorization to retry.

Integration status is `pass`, `fail`, `unavailable`, `not_performed` or
`not_in_scope`. Its summary is required and bounded to 600 characters; evidence
uses the same file-reference array. The report labels this block `agent_authored`.
A claimed integration pass does not establish a stored verdict or artistic acceptance.

The complete caller block must encode to at most 8192 bytes as finite UTF-8 JSON
with compact separators. Oversized or malformed blocks, unreadable files and
hash mismatches fail before a new handoff is published. Detailed observations
belong in linked files or the existing unrestricted expert details, not truncated
inside the compact block. `pixl.caller_result.CALLER_SCHEMA` describes the shape.

## Returned facts and exact retrieval

Caller view retains every default receipt field (`path`, `sha256`, `asset_id`,
`requirements_hash`, `state_hash`, `next`, `scope`) and adds:

- `assignment`: the supplied status and its `agent_authored` basis.
- `caller`: presence, authored fields and the file-verification observation.
- `production`: captured task ID/state, selection currency, criterion counts for
  current nominees, job counts and delivery facts. Unperformed/unavailable checks
  remain unresolved. Counts never imply every operation or visual check succeeded.
- `store`: the exact continuation's project-relative production store.
- `details_ref` and `resume_ref`: immutable file path/hash, physical line range,
  UTF-8 byte count and JSON pointer for the saved section.
- `resume_inline`, `resume_bytes`, and the unchanged `resume` when it occupies at
  most 4096 compact UTF-8 JSON bytes. Larger continuations are omitted as a whole
  and remain retrievable through `resume_ref`; there is no partial rewritten resume.
- `refresh`: the exact focused `pixl_plar_read` operation and arguments. Reread
  after state or source changes and compare requirements/state identities before
  acting. This operation is a read instruction, not automatic execution.

Delivery remains exactly the existing handoff's derived delivery value. If larger
than 2048 compact JSON bytes, `production.delivery_inline` is false and
`delivery_ref` identifies `/resume/delivery`; the containing resume line range is
returned intact. `delivery_complete` and `delivery_observed` remain visible.
Destination bytes and declared family criteria do not establish undeclared engine
or artistic checks. Assignment status remains independent even when delivery is
complete or an external destination subsequently changes without a state revision.

Use existing `source` / `pixl_source` with the locator's path, SHA-256, line bounds
and an adequate byte budget. The field slice is exact JSON source text and can
include its trailing object-member comma. The JSON pointer identifies its meaning;
no new reader tool is required. A larger section may be read in smaller physical
line ranges under the same file hash. When parsing as an object, open the complete
immutable file or wrap the returned member after removing its trailing comma.

Caller-view errors use `caller_result_input`, `caller_result_size`,
`caller_artifact_unavailable` and `caller_artifact_stale`; existing `path_escape`,
`handoff_stale`, `handoff_state` and `handoff_corrupt` retain their meaning. A file
failure identifies the declared file's `path` and `expected_file_sha256`; a hash
mismatch also returns `observed_file_sha256`. Its allocation `plar_path` stays
separate from that artifact path in structured diagnostics. A file
export failure does not undo an already saved handoff. Reconcile its returned
operation result before repeating the save; never treat it as a reason to repeat
remote generation.

1	# Request and criteria handoff
2	
3	Use for delegated asset work when a proposed production contract is ready to adopt, or when its consequential request/criteria change. The specialist prepares the contract; the calling agent independently compares its actual contents to the original assignment. This is an agent-to-agent review, not a new user-approval gate. Continue under established authorization when the contract is consistent.
4	
5	## Specialist: return the exact proposed contract
6	
7	Use the focused authoring context described in [family delivery](family-delivery.md)
8	to locate current records before exploring histories. Keep a proposal's shared
9	source index once and reference its entries from individual clauses; preserve each
10	clause's authority, scope and exact locator. Do not duplicate whole reports in
11	every criterion, abbreviate literal checks into a group summary, or treat the
12	index's source class as requirement authority. Read the original source text for
13	the comparison; retrieve a complete record/history only where it bears on the
14	decision. Exact connected review remains the handoff for adoption.
15	
16	For a connected family/stage plan, use the adapter's returned `request_review`
17	arguments and retain that exact report as described in
18	[the connected handoff](#connected-family-and-stage-handoff). It supplies the saved
19	criteria and request evidence without manually rebuilding a candidate packet.
20	
21	For other contracts, save a compact `request-review.json` in the consumer project. Point to existing artifacts instead of duplicating provider history or manufacturing PX2 state for a planning-only task. Its fields are:
22	
23	- `version`: 1.
24	- `sources`: the brief and relevant consumer/reference sources, each with project-relative `path`, actual byte `sha256`, and `role`; include locators for the adopted decisions. Numbered locators refer to that individual file, never a concatenated multi-file terminal display. The caller verifies the cited content at those locators. Include the selected `requirements_hash` when PLAR supplied one.
25	- `request`: `path`, `sha256`, `kind` (`provider_arguments` or `creative_brief`) and the actual tool name when known. Provider arguments must be the complete exact JSON to dispatch, including real reference inputs. Use a creative brief when an operation/schema has not been discovered; do not label it executable.
26	- `criteria`: `path` and `sha256` for the exact criteria to use. Each criterion has an ID, check, authority/basis, applicable scope and source locator. Distinguish owner/consumer requirements, specialist sample choices, observations and diagnostics.
27	- `choices`: the consequential specialist choices or unresolved decisions, where each appears in the request/criteria, and its reason. A criterion scoped to a chosen sample can assess that sample; it does not establish a universal project requirement.
28	- `resume`: existing store/task/output/job links when applicable. Omit absent production state.
29	
30	Return the packet's path and SHA-256 to the caller. For PX2 production, link the saved request and Q records or an exact exported view with their state/record identity. Do not silently rebuild the request after review. Before dispatch, compare the actual arguments to the reviewed request; reference bytes/handles and non-text controls matter as much as prompt wording.
31	
32	Keep a required outcome separate from the recipe proposed to achieve it. A qualitative requirement such as matching a reference or conveying a state still needs an acceptance criterion when its palette, geometry, frame count or layout are open. When demoting an unsupported recipe to a sample choice, preserve the underlying required outcome; do not leave only mechanical checks binding. Consumer code establishes its actual data/rendering behavior, not an unmeasured aesthetic quality. Attribute expert quality criteria to expert judgment where that is their basis.
33	
34	Creative decisions within the assignment need not all go back to the user. For example, choosing a static first sample or a construction method is expert judgment; attributing it to an owner who specified only canvas dimensions is incorrect. Keep the choice explicit and scoped so it can be revised without changing the owner's brief. Observations alone do not become rejection rules.
35	
36	### Measured facts in creative requests
37	
38	Do not estimate pixel coordinates by eye and then describe them as verified. When a numerical image fact materially guides a request or verdict, retain the measurement with its source-image hash, frame and coordinate convention. The existing `asset-check --regions COLOR...` / `pixl_asset_check(regions=[...])` measures exact RGBA component boxes; it does not identify the subject or make those colors mandatory. Boxes use zero-based coordinates with exclusive right/bottom edges. For other measurements, save the reproducible calculation. When exact coordinates are unnecessary, describe the visual relationship and supply the actual reference instead.
39	
40	Keep centering calculations in one coordinate convention. For a half-open box
41	`[left, top, right, bottom]`, its centre in pixel-edge coordinates is
42	`((left + right) / 2, (top + bottom) / 2)` and the canvas centre is `(width / 2, height / 2)`.
43	A centroid computed from zero-based pixel indices needs `+0.5` per axis to use those
44	same edge coordinates. A margin imbalance, box-centre offset and mass-centroid offset
45	are different quantities; retain the actual calculation before calling an asset centred.
46	
47	The caller independently verifies consequential measured claims against the original image and measurement, including the coordinate convention; repeating a specialist's pixel map is not independent verification. Correct unsupported numbers before dispatch while preserving the required visual outcome.

128	### Compare the original sources and exact contract
129	
130	For either route, open the retained packet/report and verify its hashes. Read the original brief, relevant sources, complete request and complete criteria, not just the specialist's summary or self-audit. Check:
131	
132	1. Every explicit requirement survives into the request and relevant checks, including qualitative identity/style/state outcomes, actual reference role/input and consumer mapping. Check for dropped or weakened outcomes as well as added restrictions.
133	2. Every consequential extra restriction has its true basis and scope. Test whether a brief-conforming alternative would be rejected only because an observation or proposal was promoted to an owner requirement.
134	3. The proposed operation's actual declaration supports the payload. Do not infer a provider parameter, frame/direction count, alpha policy or camera from prose alone.
135	4. Findings concern these exact artifacts. Mechanical/hash validity and a specialist's consistency claim do not prove semantic agreement or artistic quality.
136	5. Each rejection rule belongs to the current candidate/stage and has satisfiable prerequisites. A first sample cannot require completed dependent family assets before it may be accepted. Retain deferred family or destination obligations with an explicit later stage in the handoff/PLAR; verify they remain scheduled rather than dropping the required outcome.
137	
138	For each rejection criterion, save one concise comparison using the following
139	sequence. A table or JSON is sufficient; this is the caller's actual reasoning about
140	the source, not a worksheet to have the specialist certify for itself.
141	
142	1. **Source obligation.** Derive the minimum required outcome from the original source
143	   wording and locator before using the draft criterion as its paraphrase. State what
144	   the source leaves open. For an expert criterion, identify the actual expert choice
145	   and candidate scope instead of inventing owner authority.
146	2. **Literal condition and additions.** Compare the entire check with that obligation.
147	   Identify the exact added or omitted words/clauses, including extent, composition,
148	   exclusions, comparisons and numerical bounds. A supported noun does not establish
149	   support for its modifiers. Read the check itself, not just its basis or label.
150	3. **Discriminating alternative.** For each added restriction, describe a plausible
151	   asset that keeps the source obligation true while making that specific restriction
152	   false. Name the clause being tested and whether the literal check would reject it.
153	   Merely changing a value the check already permits does not test that restriction.
154	   If the source itself excludes the alternative, identify the exact source support.
155	4. **Disposition.** Keep the required outcome; remove an unsupported narrowing from
156	   that rule or split it into an explicitly scoped expert choice with its own rationale.
157	   An ambiguous condition that could reject a valid alternative needs clearer wording;
158	   do not approve it by silently giving it a more permissive interpretation. Verify the
159	   correction in the returned artifact before marking the contract consistent.
160	
161	For example, a requirement for a readable silhouette does not itself require an
162	outlined silhouette. Comparing two outline colours leaves the added outline rule
163	untested; a readable outline-free construction tests it. The specialist may still
164	recommend an outline for this sample and explain its artistic value. The comparison
165	preserves that expertise while accurately describing who chose it and what it binds.
166	
167	Cover every rejection rule; group only genuinely identical ones. Retain the source
168	quote/bounds, literal delta, tested alternative and disposition together. A general
169	"the brief permits flexibility" statement or a prompt-choice label elsewhere cannot
170	cancel a restriction still present in an owner-authority acceptance condition.
171	
172	Check the **review route** as well as the wording. A local mechanical check can
173	establish measured dimensions, frame counts or alpha values. It cannot decide which
174	shape is intentional foreground, whether a matte is unwanted, whether a silhouette
175	reads as the requested symbol, or whether an accent serves its role. For a mixed
176	criterion, either split the measurement and required visual judgment or set its mode
177	to `visual` (normally domain `visual` too). The runtime requires saved native/enlarged
178	candidate views for visual-mode or visual/continuity-domain reviews; labelling such a
179	condition `mechanical`/`local` bypasses that evidence requirement. A planning-only
180	correction must still specify the route its future acceptance will actually need.
181	Do not call a corrected contract operable merely because its source locators resolve.
182	
183	When reviewing a specialist's response to a discrepancy, re-open the literal check.
184	An added attribution or a claim that a conventional construction excludes no valid
185	alternatives does not remove an unchanged mandatory recipe. Retain the source's
186	qualitative outcome as required and place the expert construction in a scoped proposal;
187	judge actual recognizability without declaring one geometric recipe universal.
188	
189	Resolve every evidence-report diagnostic before calling a locator verified. For a
190	text citation, open the actual source, use its file-local inclusive bounds and save
191	those bounds in the corrected packet; a nearby matching sentence does not repair a
192	wrong range. An unresolved named or visual reference needs actual inspection and a
193	recorded finding. A source hash alone never verifies the cited location or its meaning.
194	
195	The [delegation boundary](delegation.md#caller--specialist) distinguishes unchanged
196	historical evidence from the editable corrected proposal. A caller must not freeze
197	prior criterion text or authority in the new proposal; reassess those interpretations
198	against the source. Use the profile's visual-role distinctions when translating colour,
199	subject construction and transparency intent, rather than adding a construction rule.
200	
201	If a contract defect is found after delivery, preserve the original request, plan,
202	verdicts and candidate. Save a corrected proposal and independent comparison as a new
203	artifact, explicitly distinguishing it from the historical contract used for delivery.
204	Do not create another provider job merely to correct documentation, transplant old
205	verdicts to new criteria, or silently rewrite durable completed work. Carry both the
206	historical identity and the correction's adoption scope in the exact handoff details.
207	
208	Keep process requirements, output requirements and diagnostic proxies distinct. A required production route is checked through actual calls and downloaded-byte provenance; a property of the resulting image is evidence only when it establishes that claim. Do not silently turn a process restriction into an extra output-difference test, or a diagnostic into a rejection rule. Independent review uses the original source, not another agent's assertion that the rule is sourced.
209	
210	Save a concise `caller-review.json` (or equivalent named fields) with reviewer role, reviewed packet hash, `consistent` / `changes_requested` / `needs_input`, per-criterion comparisons and other findings tied to request locations and source evidence, and the next action. `consistent` means the planned contract matches this assignment; it is not provider execution or asset acceptance.
211	
212	If changes are needed, send the specialist the precise discrepancy and relevant source; preserve the original artifacts, revise only the affected contract, and inspect the returned new packet. Reuse the existing specialist when the host supports it. Resolve supplied facts yourself; ask the user only a consequential decision genuinely missing from the available context. No token, secret header or credential belongs in either file.
213	
214	If no independent caller/reviewer exists, retain the specialist's own review as self-review, proceed within existing authorization, and report the independent comparison as unperformed. Do not invent another agent or stop ordinary direct work solely to satisfy this procedure.

216	## Carry the comparison through production
217	
218	Return `request_review` in the normal result, containing the packet and caller-review paths/hashes and unresolved findings. After preparing the durable provider job, verify its actual request still matches the reviewed arguments. A changed requirement, criterion or request needs a new comparison; polling progress and unrelated queue changes do not.
219	
220	The final caller opens the delivered assets, checks the actual request and output against this contract, and records its own observations. Keep contract consistency, provider outcome, visual quality and destination acceptance separate. For a rejected candidate, retain the failure and the revised request/criteria; changing a checker merely to pass the candidate is a contract change, not an asset correction.

222	When an artistic explanation asserts a measurement, compare that assertion with
223	its actual data and coordinate convention. Reproducing a bounding box does not
224	verify a stated axis angle or arm-length ratio; approximate visual descriptions
225	should remain approximate. Correct an inconsistent explanation in a new observation
226	without converting its sample geometry into an additional rejection condition.
227	Reassess the original claim using its stated inputs. For quoted endpoints, retain
228	the coordinate convention and calculate their deltas, lengths and angles before
229	confirming an axis or ratio. Counts of occupied pixels, a bounding box and a newly

1	# Compact caller result
2	
3	`plar handoff DETAILS_JSON --view caller` / `pixl_plar_handoff` with
4	`view: "caller"` saves the existing immutable version-1 handoff, then returns a
5	bounded presentation of that same captured selection. The default `view: "receipt"`
6	and saved bytes for identical inputs are unchanged. There is no new ledger, UDL
7	record, provider action or acceptance event.
8	
9	## Agent-authored compact fields
10	
11	`details.status` retains its existing assignment meaning: `delivered`, `partial`,
12	`needs_input` or `blocked`. It does not follow automatically from production state.
13	An optional `details.caller` object supplies the following closed fields:
14	
15	| Field | Content |
16	| --- | --- |
17	| `summary` | Nonempty text, at most 600 characters |
18	| `artifacts` | At most 12 actual project file references |
19	| `reports` | At most 12 references to separately retained detailed reports |
20	| `issues` | At most 12 objects with `category`, `summary` and optional `recovery` |
21	| `integration` | An agent observation with `status`, `summary` and optional `evidence` file references |
22	
23	All fields are optional. Omission means not reported, not a pass or an unavailable
24	check. An absent caller block is returned as `caller.present: false`; arbitrary
25	legacy details are never heuristically summarized. Existing receipt mode does not
26	reinterpret a legacy field called `caller`.
27	
28	File references contain exactly `path`, `sha256` and `role`. Paths are nonempty
29	forward-slash project-relative paths, at most 512 characters. SHA-256 is 64 lowercase
30	hexadecimal digits; role is nonempty text of at most 96 characters. The operation
31	confines and hashes every declared artifact, report and integration-evidence file
32	before publishing. It does not copy those files or guarantee that they remain
33	unchanged after that observation. Roles and judgments are supplied by the agent.
34	
35	Issue categories are `invalid_authoring`, `stale_local_state`, `missing_capability`,
36	`uncertain_remote_result`, `unavailable_observation` and `unfinished_work`.
37	Summary and recovery text each have the same 600-character bound. The category is
38	an agent's classification, not an automatic diagnosis or authorization to retry.
39	
40	Integration status is `pass`, `fail`, `unavailable`, `not_performed` or
41	`not_in_scope`. Its summary is required and bounded to 600 characters; evidence
42	uses the same file-reference array. The report labels this block `agent_authored`.
43	A claimed integration pass does not establish a stored verdict or artistic acceptance.
44	
45	The complete caller block must encode to at most 8192 bytes as finite UTF-8 JSON
46	with compact separators. Oversized or malformed blocks, unreadable files and
47	hash mismatches fail before a new handoff is published. Detailed observations
48	belong in linked files or the existing unrestricted expert details, not truncated
49	inside the compact block. `pixl.caller_result.CALLER_SCHEMA` describes the shape.
50	
51	## Returned facts and exact retrieval
52	
53	Caller view retains every default receipt field (`path`, `sha256`, `asset_id`,
54	`requirements_hash`, `state_hash`, `next`, `scope`) and adds:
55	
56	- `assignment`: the supplied status and its `agent_authored` basis.
57	- `caller`: presence, authored fields and the file-verification observation.
58	- `production`: captured task ID/state, selection currency, criterion counts for
59	  current nominees, job counts and delivery facts. Unperformed/unavailable checks
60	  remain unresolved. Counts never imply every operation or visual check succeeded.
61	- `store`: the exact continuation's project-relative production store.
62	- `details_ref` and `resume_ref`: immutable file path/hash, physical line range,
63	  UTF-8 byte count and JSON pointer for the saved section.
64	- `resume_inline`, `resume_bytes`, and the unchanged `resume` when it occupies at
65	  most 4096 compact UTF-8 JSON bytes. Larger continuations are omitted as a whole
66	  and remain retrievable through `resume_ref`; there is no partial rewritten resume.
67	- `refresh`: the exact focused `pixl_plar_read` operation and arguments. Reread
68	  after state or source changes and compare requirements/state identities before
69	  acting. This operation is a read instruction, not automatic execution.
70	
71	Delivery remains exactly the existing handoff's derived delivery value. If larger
72	than 2048 compact JSON bytes, `production.delivery_inline` is false and
73	`delivery_ref` identifies `/resume/delivery`; the containing resume line range is
74	returned intact. `delivery_complete` and `delivery_observed` remain visible.
75	Destination bytes and declared family criteria do not establish undeclared engine
76	or artistic checks. Assignment status remains independent even when delivery is
77	complete or an external destination subsequently changes without a state revision.
78	
79	Use existing `source` / `pixl_source` with the locator's path, SHA-256, line bounds
80	and an adequate byte budget. The field slice is exact JSON source text and can
81	include its trailing object-member comma. The JSON pointer identifies its meaning;
82	no new reader tool is required. A larger section may be read in smaller physical
83	line ranges under the same file hash. When parsing as an object, open the complete
84	immutable file or wrap the returned member after removing its trailing comma.
85	
86	Caller-view errors use `caller_result_input`, `caller_result_size`,
87	`caller_artifact_unavailable` and `caller_artifact_stale`; existing `path_escape`,
88	`handoff_stale`, `handoff_state` and `handoff_corrupt` retain their meaning. A file
89	failure identifies the declared file's `path` and `expected_file_sha256`; a hash
90	mismatch also returns `observed_file_sha256`. Its allocation `plar_path` stays
91	separate from that artifact path in structured diagnostics. A file
92	export failure does not undo an already saved handoff. Reconcile its returned
93	operation result before repeating the save; never treat it as a reason to repeat
94	remote generation.

cd "/c/Users/ryanf/AppData/Local/Temp/pixl readiness claude clean h0x5smz6/consumer" && "C:/github/pixel-lab-agent/build/readiness-setup-01/runtime/Scripts/python.exe" -I - <<'EOF'
from PIL import Image, ImageOps
import hashlib
def info(p):
    im=Image.open(p).convert('RGBA'); px=im.load(); w,h=im.size
    vis=[(x,y) for y in range(h) for x in range(w) if px[x,y][3]>0]
    frac=sum(1 for x,y in vis if 0<px[x,y][3]<255)
    cols=sorted(set('#%02x%02x%02x'%px[x,y][:3] for x,y in vis))
    xs=[x for x,_ in vis]; ys=[y for _,y in vis]
    print(p, im.size, im.mode, 'vis',len(vis),'frac',frac,'bbox',[min(xs),min(ys),max(xs)+1,max(ys)+1],'centre',(min(xs)+max(xs)+1)/2, cols)
    return im
for p in ['work/native-production/returned/rotations/east.png','work/native-production/returned/rotations/north.png','work/native-production/returned/rotations/west.png','work/native-production/edited/west-mirror-of-east.png']:
    info(p)
e=Image.open('work/native-production/returned/rotations/east.png').convert('RGBA')
we=Image.open('work/native-production/edited/west-mirror-of-east.png').convert('RGBA')
wr=Image.open('work/native-production/returned/rotations/west.png').convert('RGBA')
print('mirror(east)==edited west:', ImageOps.mirror(e).tobytes()==we.tobytes())
d=[(x,y) for y in range(32) for x in range(32) if we.getpixel((x,y))!=wr.getpixel((x,y))]
print('edited vs raw west diff count', len(d), d[:3], d[-3:])
n=Image.open('work/native-production/returned/rotations/north.png').convert('RGBA'); s=Image.open('assets/robot-base.png').convert('RGBA')
print('north alpha == south alpha:', n.getchannel('A').tobytes()==s.getchannel('A').tobytes())
for name,im in (('east',e),('west-raw',wr)):
    px=im.load()
    print(name); 
    for y in range(32):
        print('%2d '%y+''.join('.' if px[x,y][3]==0 else ('F' if px[x,y][:3]==(37,53,74) else ('B' if px[x,y][:3]==(86,181,188) else 'E')) for x in range(32)))
EOF
